title: Greek Mythology: Figures, Relationships and Story Cycles
description: The Hellenic pantheon mapped as a relationship graph: primordials, Titans, Olympians, chthonic powers, heroes and monsters, with every figure traced to Hesiod, Homer, the Homeric Hymns, Apollodorus, Ovid or Pausanias.
sources: Hesiod, Theogony and Works and Days (Evelyn-White, 1914)
Encyclopaedia Britannica and Wikipedia for cross-checking dates and cult sites
portraitNote: Portraits are original illustrations in a single uniform style for the whole pack, stored locally in the portraits/greek/ folder. No images are fetched from the network.

profile.cosmicNature: Linear and declining. Hesiod sets out five Ages of Man - Golden, Silver, Bronze, Heroic and Iron - falling away from an easy beginning toward the hard present, with no promised renewal. Time moves forward and conditions worsen; there is no wheel of ages to come round again.
profile.natureOfDivinity: Anthropomorphic. The gods are deathless and vastly powerful but recognisably person-shaped: they quarrel, take sides, hold grudges, are wounded, and are bound by oaths on the Styx. They are not the ground of being and did not make the cosmos; they inherited it by conquest and hold it as a dynasty.
profile.afterlife: A shared shade-existence rather than reward. Nearly everyone goes to the house of Hades as a witless shade; only the exceptional are exempted, to Elysium or the Isles of the Blest, and only the exceptionally guilty are punished in Tartarus. Judgment by Minos, Rhadamanthys and Aeacus is a later, largely Platonic elaboration.
profile.systemMechanism: A dynastic patriarchal monarchy forged by generational warfare. Ouranos is overthrown by Cronus, Cronus by Zeus in the ten-year Titanomachy, after which the three brothers divide the cosmos by lot into sky, sea and the world below. Zeus rules from Olympus, enforcing oath-keeping and hospitality, while Fate stands above even him.
profile.canonTexts: Hesiod's Theogony and Works and Days, the Iliad and Odyssey, the Homeric Hymns, the Athenian tragedians, Apollodorus' Library and Ovid's Metamorphoses as later systematising compilations.

hierarchy.title: Primordial Forces
hierarchy.blurb: The first beings, who come into existence rather than being made. None of them creates the world deliberately; they simply are, and the world proceeds from what they generate.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Gaia and Ouranos parent the Titan dynasty

hierarchy.title: The Titan Dynasty
hierarchy.blurb: Twelve children of Earth and Sky, hidden away by their father until Cronus took the sickle. They ruled from Mount Othrys for an age, and all but Oceanus lost the war that ended it.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Overthrown in the ten-year Titanomachy; the cosmos divided by lot

hierarchy.title: The Tripartite Rulers
hierarchy.blurb: After the war the three brothers drew lots for the cosmos: sky, sea and the world below, with earth and Olympus held in common. This division, not creation, is the basis of Olympian authority.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Zeus rules from Olympus, bound by oath and by Fate

hierarchy.title: The Olympian Court
hierarchy.blurb: The twelve who sit on Olympus, holding the settled offices of the new order: war and wisdom, craft and desire, the harvest, the hearth, the message and the vine.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Beneath them, the powers of fate and of the dead, which the Olympians do not command

hierarchy.title: Chthonic Powers & Fate
hierarchy.blurb: The older authorities that the Olympian settlement did not abolish. The Moirai bind even Zeus, the Erinyes answer to no one, and the house of Hades keeps whatever enters it.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: On earth, heroes clear the monsters and the epics happen

hierarchy.title: Heroes, Mortals & Monsters
hierarchy.blurb: The generation in which gods and mortals still mix directly. Heroes fathered by gods clear the monstrous children of Typhon and Echidna, and the Theban and Trojan cycles run their course.

stories.title: The Coming of the First Beings
stories.summary: Hesiod's account of how things began. Chaos comes into being first, and after it broad-breasted Gaia, dim Tartaros and Eros, fairest of the deathless gods and the loosener of limbs. From Chaos come Erebos and black Night, and from their union Aither and Day. Gaia then bears, without any partner, the starry sky Ouranos to cover her and be a home for the blessed gods, the mountains, and Pontos the barren sea. There is no maker and no plan: the first beings simply come to be, and generate their own opposites. Night alone produces a catalogue of dooms - Death, Sleep, Blame, the Fates, Nemesis, Strife - and the shape of the world is set before any god has ruled it.

stories.title: The Sickle of Adamant
stories.summary: Ouranos hates his children from the first and pushes each one back inside Gaia as it is born, so that the earth groans with being overfull. Gaia makes a great sickle of grey adamant and asks her sons which of them will act; all are afraid except Cronus, the youngest and most terrible, who takes it. Gaia hides him in ambush, and when Ouranos comes down over the earth Cronus cuts off his genitals and throws them behind him without looking. From the blood that falls on the earth come the Erinyes, the Giants and the Meliae; from the foam that gathers about the flesh in the sea comes Aphrodite. Ouranos, mutilated, gives with Gaia the prophecy that Cronus in his turn will be overcome by his own son.

stories.title: Cronus Swallows His Children
stories.summary: Warned by Gaia and Ouranos that his own son will overcome him, Cronus swallows each child Rhea bears as soon as it is born: Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades and Poseidon in turn. Pregnant with her sixth, Rhea appeals to her parents, who send her to Lyctus on Crete. She bears Zeus there by night and gives him to Gaia to hide in a cave, and hands Cronus a great stone wrapped in swaddling clothes, which he swallows without looking, believing it is the child. The infant is nursed in hiding while armed Kouretes clash their shields so his crying cannot be heard. Grown, Zeus forces his father to disgorge first the stone, which is set at Delphi as a sign, and then his brothers and sisters, alive and undamaged.

stories.title: The Ten-Year War
stories.summary: The Olympians hold Olympus and the Titans hold Othrys, and for ten years neither side can gain the advantage. Gaia tells Zeus that victory lies with the prisoners in the earth. He goes down and revives the Cyclopes and the Hundred-Handers with nectar and ambrosia; the Cyclopes give him the thunderbolt, Poseidon the trident and Hades the helm of invisibility, and the Hundred-Handers throw three hundred rocks at once and bury the Titans beneath them. The Titans are confined in Tartaros with the Hundred-Handers as their guards. Atlas, as their leader, is given a different sentence: to stand at the western edge of the world holding the sky apart from the earth. Oceanus, who took no part, is left alone.

stories.title: Zeus and Typhon
stories.summary: Gaia's answer to the defeat of the Titans is her last child, Typhon, fathered by Tartaros: a creature with a hundred serpent heads whose voices bellow, roar, yelp and hiss. Hesiod says that had Zeus not acted at once, Typhon would have ruled gods and men. In Apollodorus' fuller version the fight goes badly first - Typhon takes Zeus, cuts the sinews from his hands and feet and hides him in a Cilician cave, until Hermes steals the sinews back and restores him. Zeus then drives him with thunderbolts across the world and finally throws Mount Etna on top of him, which is why the mountain burns. Typhon and Echidna together father most of the monsters the heroes will later have to kill.

stories.title: The Division of the Cosmos
stories.summary: With the Titans confined, the three sons of Cronus divide what they have won. Poseidon describes the arrangement himself in the Iliad: three brothers born of Cronus and Rhea, and all things divided into three, each receiving his own domain. He shook the lots and drew the grey sea to live in for ever; Hades drew the misty darkness; Zeus drew the wide sky among the clouds and the bright air. The earth and high Olympus were left common to all three. Poseidon raises the division precisely to argue that Zeus, though eldest in honour, has no authority to order him about - which is the tradition's clearest statement that Olympian rule rests on a shared settlement after a war, not on any god having made the world.

stories.title: The Theft of Fire
stories.summary: At Mecone, when gods and men are settling their portions, Prometheus divides a great ox into two and hides the meat under the ugly stomach and the bare bones under glistening fat, then invites Zeus to choose. Zeus takes the fat, and from then on men keep the meat and burn the bones for the gods. In return Zeus withholds fire, and Prometheus steals it back in the hollow of a fennel stalk. His punishment is to be bound to a crag where an eagle eats his liver each day and it grows back each night. Aeschylus adds that Prometheus also knows a secret Zeus needs - which marriage would produce a son greater than his father - and will not tell it. Generations later Heracles shoots the eagle and frees him.

stories.title: The Making of Pandora
stories.summary: Zeus answers the theft of fire with a gift. Hephaestus moulds a woman from earth and water; Athena teaches her weaving and dresses her; Aphrodite gives grace and aching longing; Hermes gives her a shameless mind and deceitful words; and each god adds something, which is what her name records. She is sent to Epimetheus, who accepts her although his brother warned him never to take anything from Zeus. She lifts the lid of a great storage jar, and out come the sicknesses, sorrows and hard labours that had not existed before, scattering beyond recall. Only Hope remains inside, caught under the rim, and Hesiod does not say whether that is mercy or the last cruelty - a question readers have argued over ever since.

stories.title: The Five Ages
stories.summary: Hesiod sets out the history of humankind as a decline through five ages. The golden race lived under Cronus without toil or old age, and the earth gave freely; they became kindly spirits watching over mortals. The silver race were foolish and refused the gods honour, and Zeus put them away. The bronze race were terrible and warlike and destroyed themselves. Then, breaking the pattern of metals, came the race of heroes, better and more just, who fought at Thebes and at Troy and some of whom live still in the Isles of the Blest. Last is the iron race, Hesiod's own, who labour and grieve by day and die by night, and whose end will come when children are born already grey. Time in this scheme moves one way, and it moves downward.

stories.title: Athena from the Head of Zeus
stories.summary: Zeus takes Metis, wisest of gods and men, as his first wife. Gaia and Ouranos warn him that she is fated to bear first a daughter of equal spirit and then a son who would be king of gods and men, so Zeus tricks her into becoming small and swallows her, taking her counsel into himself. The child grows inside him until his head splits - in most accounts Hephaestus opens it with an axe - and Athena leaps out fully armed, with a war cry that shakes Olympus. It is the only place in the succession sequence where the pattern of a son overthrowing his father is broken, and it is broken by anticipation: Zeus does not defeat the prophecy, he absorbs the mother and prevents the son from being conceived.

stories.title: Leto and the Island of Delos
stories.summary: Leto, pregnant by Zeus, is refused a birthplace by every land, because all of them fear Hera. Only Delos will take her, a small floating island of no consequence, and only on the condition that Apollo will build his temple there; the island is thereafter anchored to the sea floor. Even so the labour lasts nine days and nights, because Hera keeps Eileithyia, the goddess of childbirth, beside her on Olympus and does not let her go. The other goddesses send Iris with a necklace nine cubits long as a bribe, and Eileithyia comes. Artemis is born first and, in a detail the tradition keeps, helps at the birth of her brother. Apollo, tasting nectar, at once claims the lyre, the bow and the giving of oracles as his own.

stories.title: Hermes Steals Apollo's Cattle
stories.summary: Born at dawn in a cave on Cyllene, Hermes is out of his cradle by midday. He finds a tortoise at the door, kills it and makes the first lyre from its shell, then goes out and takes fifty of Apollo's cattle, driving them backwards so that the tracks lead the wrong way and wearing brushwood sandals to disguise his own. He sacrifices two, divides the meat into twelve portions for the twelve gods, and is back in his swaddling clothes by evening. Apollo tracks him down and brings him before Zeus, where Hermes lies so charmingly that Zeus laughs out loud. The quarrel is settled by trade: Hermes gives Apollo the lyre and keeps the cattle, and the two are friends afterwards.

stories.title: The Taking of Persephone
stories.summary: Persephone is gathering flowers in a meadow when she reaches for a narcissus; the earth opens and Hades takes her below in his chariot, with Zeus' consent. Demeter searches for nine days with torches, eating nothing, and Hecate goes with her; on the tenth Helios tells her what happened and who allowed it. She leaves Olympus in fury, comes to Eleusis as an old woman, and finally withholds the grain altogether, so that nothing grows and humankind faces extinction while the gods face the end of sacrifice. Zeus is forced to negotiate. Persephone is returned, but she has eaten pomegranate seeds below, and whoever eats there belongs there, so she must go back for part of each year. Before leaving, Demeter teaches the Eleusinians her rites.

stories.title: Athena and Poseidon Contest Athens
stories.summary: Two gods claim the new city of Attica, and the matter is put to a contest of gifts. Poseidon strikes the rock of the Acropolis with his trident and brings out a spring of salt water - or, in another account, produces the first horse. Athena plants an olive tree. The gods, or the twelve Olympians, or Cecrops the first king, judge the olive the more useful gift, because it gives food, oil and wood, and the city takes her name. Poseidon, slighted, floods the Thriasian plain. Both marks were shown on the Acropolis for centuries afterwards: a salt spring and the sacred olive, which was said to have burned in the Persian sack and to have put out a new shoot the next day.

stories.title: The Net of Hephaestus
stories.summary: Helios, who sees everything, tells Hephaestus that his wife Aphrodite has been sleeping with Ares. Hephaestus goes to his forge and makes a net of chains finer than spider-silk and invisible even to gods, fixes it over the bed, and announces he is going to Lemnos. Ares comes at once; the two are caught fast, and Hephaestus calls the gods in to see. The male gods crowd the doorway and laugh, and Apollo asks Hermes whether he would take the chains for the sake of lying beside golden Aphrodite, and Hermes says he would take three times as many. Poseidon alone does not laugh, and negotiates their release by guaranteeing that Ares will pay the fine. Ares goes to Thrace and Aphrodite to Cyprus.

stories.title: The Golden Throne
stories.summary: Cast out of Olympus by Hera for his lameness, Hephaestus takes his revenge by craft. He makes a golden throne of great beauty and sends it to her as a gift; when she sits in it, invisible bonds hold her fast, and no god can free her. Ares goes to fetch him back by force and is driven off with firebrands. Dionysus succeeds where Ares failed by getting the smith thoroughly drunk and bringing him home slumped on the back of a donkey, a scene Greek vase painters returned to again and again. Hephaestus releases Hera on his own terms, and is restored to Olympus. The story is one of the tradition's clearest statements that craft and patience beat force.

stories.title: The Twice-Born
stories.summary: Semele, a Theban princess, is pregnant by Zeus. Hera comes to her disguised as an old nurse and plants a doubt: is her lover really the god he says he is? Semele asks Zeus for a promise before naming her request, and he swears by the Styx; she then asks him to appear as he appears to Hera. Bound by an oath no god can break, he comes in lightning, and she is destroyed. Zeus snatches the unborn child from the fire and sews it into his own thigh, from which Dionysus is born at term - the second birth that gives him his title. Raised in hiding from Hera, he later goes down to the underworld and brings Semele up, making her a goddess under the name Thyone.

stories.title: Dionysus and the Pirates
stories.summary: Tyrrhenian pirates find a handsome young man on a headland by the sea and seize him, expecting a rich ransom, though the helmsman warns that this is no ordinary passenger and that the ropes will not hold him. They do not hold him. Wine begins to run through the ship, a vine spreads over the sail, ivy winds up the mast, and the god shows himself as a lion. The crew leap overboard in terror and become dolphins; only the helmsman, who spoke for him, is spared and told who he has carried. It is the standard shape of a Dionysus story in miniature: the god arrives unrecognised, is refused, and the refusal is answered not with argument but with a demonstration nobody can misunderstand.

stories.title: The Children of Niobe
stories.summary: Niobe, queen of Thebes, has seven sons and seven daughters, and interrupts a sacrifice to Leto to ask why the city honours a goddess with only two children when she herself has fourteen. Apollo and Artemis answer within the hour: he shoots the sons, she shoots the daughters, and in most versions every one of them dies. Niobe weeps until she is turned to stone on Mount Sipylus, and the rock still seeps water. The story is the tradition's most economical statement about hybris in the specific sense the Greeks meant - not pride in general, but a mortal setting their own good fortune beside a god's and drawing a comparison. Niobe says nothing untrue; the count is correct. That is not the point.

stories.title: Apollo and Daphne
stories.summary: Apollo, fresh from killing the serpent Python, mocks Eros for playing with a bow he is too small for. Eros answers with two arrows: a gold one, sharp and bright, which he shoots into Apollo, and a blunt lead one, which he shoots into the nymph Daphne, so that the god must love and the nymph must refuse. Apollo pursues her through the woods, calling out that he is no enemy, that he is the lord of Delphi, that she does not know who is chasing her. She runs until she is exhausted and prays to her father, the river Peneus, to destroy the form that has caused this. Bark closes over her, her hair becomes leaves and her feet take root. Apollo takes the laurel as his own tree.

stories.title: The Weaving of Arachne
stories.summary: Arachne of Lydia weaves so well that people come to watch, and she says openly that she owes nothing to Athena and will compete with her. Athena comes disguised as an old woman and advises her to be more modest; Arachne tells her to keep her advice, and the goddess reveals herself. They weave. Athena's cloth shows the twelve gods in majesty and, in the four corners, mortals who challenged gods and were destroyed - a warning worked into the design. Arachne's shows god after god deceiving and assaulting mortal women, Zeus as bull and swan and shower of gold, and Ovid says plainly that the work was faultless and that neither Envy nor Athena could find anything wrong with it. Athena tears it and strikes her, and Arachne hangs herself; the goddess turns her into a spider, to hang and to spin for ever.

stories.title: Asclepius Raises the Dead
stories.summary: Asclepius, taught medicine by the centaur Chiron, becomes so skilled that he begins to bring the dead back to life - in one account using blood taken from the Gorgon's veins and given him by Athena. Hades complains that his kingdom is being emptied, and Zeus, seeing that the boundary between the living and the dead cannot be crossed without the whole order coming apart, kills Asclepius with a thunderbolt. Apollo cannot strike at Zeus, so he kills the Cyclopes who forged the bolt, and is punished with a year's servitude to the mortal king Admetus. Asclepius is afterwards raised to divine status and given the greatest healing cult in Greece, so that the story ends by granting what it began by refusing.

stories.title: Selene and the Sleeping Shepherd
stories.summary: Selene, driving her two-horse chariot across the night sky, sees a young shepherd asleep on Mount Latmos and falls in love with him. Endymion is given eternal sleep and unfading youth in a cave there - at her request in some accounts, at his own in others, since Zeus offered him whatever he wished and he asked never to grow old - and she comes down to him every night. She bears him fifty daughters, which the tradition connects to the fifty lunar months of the Olympiad cycle. It is one of very few Greek love stories with no punishment, no transformation and no loss, and the price of that is that nothing happens in it: he is preserved exactly by never waking, and she has him only on those terms.

stories.title: Eos and Tithonus
stories.summary: Eos, the Dawn, carries off the Trojan prince Tithonus and asks Zeus to make him immortal so that she will not lose him. Zeus grants it exactly as asked. She has forgotten to ask for unending youth, and so Tithonus does not die but simply continues, growing older and frailer without limit, until he cannot move and only a thin endless voice is left, and she shuts him away in a chamber behind golden doors - or, in a later version, turns him into a cicada, which sings without stopping. Their son Memnon, king of the Ethiopians, is killed by Achilles at Troy, and the morning dew was explained as Eos' tears for him. Her habit of taking mortal lovers was said to be a curse laid on her by Aphrodite.

stories.title: The Deception of Zeus
stories.summary: With the Trojans pressing the Greeks back to their ships and Zeus watching to make sure no god interferes, Hera decides to put him to sleep. She borrows the embroidered girdle of Aphrodite, which holds desire itself, on a pretext, and then goes to Hypnos and asks him to close Zeus' eyes. Hypnos refuses at first: the last time he did this for her, Zeus woke and hunted him through heaven, and he only escaped by fleeing to Night, whom Zeus would not offend. He agrees only when Hera promises him Pasithea, one of the Graces, as a wife, and makes her swear it on the Styx. Zeus sleeps; Poseidon rallies the Greeks; and when Zeus wakes the whole arrangement of the war has to be put back by force.

stories.title: Perseus and the Gorgon
stories.summary: Polydectes of Seriphos, wanting Perseus out of the way so he can take his mother Danae, demands the head of Medusa as a gift. Athena and Hermes equip him: winged sandals, the helm of invisibility, a curved sickle, a bag to hold the head, and a shield polished to a mirror. He first forces the Graeae, three sisters who share one eye and one tooth between them, to reveal the way, by snatching the eye as they pass it. Reaching the Gorgons asleep, he approaches watching only the reflection, and beheads the one of the three who can be killed. From her neck spring the winged horse Pegasus and the giant Chrysaor. He escapes invisible, and the head keeps its power: he uses it on Polydectes, then gives it to Athena for the aegis.

stories.title: Andromeda on the Rock
stories.summary: Flying home with the Gorgon's head, Perseus passes over the coast of Ethiopia and sees a girl chained to a rock at the sea's edge, so still that he takes her for a statue until the wind moves her hair. Andromeda's mother Cassiopeia had boasted that her daughter was more beautiful than the Nereids; Poseidon sent a flood and a sea monster, and an oracle said the only remedy was to give the girl to it. Perseus strikes a bargain with her parents for her hand, kills the monster, and marries her - interrupting the wedding to fight off her previous betrothed and his followers, whom he turns to stone with the head. Andromeda goes back to Greece with him, and she, Perseus, Cassiopeia and the monster are all set among the constellations.

stories.title: The Twelve Labours
stories.summary: Driven mad by Hera, Heracles kills his own wife and children, and the labours are imposed on him as expiation, set by his kinsman Eurystheus. He strangles the Nemean lion and wears its skin; burns the Hydra's necks as he cuts the heads; takes the Ceryneian hind and the Erymanthian boar alive; cleans the Augean stables in one day by diverting two rivers; drives off the Stymphalian birds; brings back the Cretan bull, the man-eating mares of Diomedes, the belt of the Amazon queen and the cattle of Geryon; fetches the golden apples of the Hesperides, tricking Atlas into taking the sky back; and finally brings Cerberus up from the underworld alive, using no weapons, and returns him. Eurystheus refused to count two of them, which is why there are twelve rather than ten.

stories.title: The Robe of Nessus
stories.summary: The centaur Nessus, ferrying Heracles' wife Deianeira across a river, tries to carry her off and is shot with an arrow poisoned by the Hydra's blood. Dying, he tells her to keep some of his blood as a love charm in case her husband's affection ever strays. Years later, hearing that Heracles is bringing home a captive princess, she soaks a robe in it and sends it to him. The poison burns into him and cannot be washed off or torn away; in agony he has a pyre built on Mount Oeta and asks to be burned alive, and only Philoctetes will light it, receiving the great bow as payment. The mortal part of him burns away, the divine part is taken up to Olympus, and Hera is reconciled to him at last and gives him Hebe in marriage.

stories.title: Theseus and the Minotaur
stories.summary: Athens, defeated by Crete, must send seven youths and seven maidens at intervals to be given to the Minotaur in the labyrinth. Theseus volunteers among them, promising his father Aegeus that he will change the ship's black sail for a white one if he lives. Minos' daughter Ariadne falls in love with him and goes to Daedalus, who tells her the secret of the maze; she gives Theseus a ball of thread to unwind on the way in and a sword, on condition that he take her with him. He kills the Minotaur, follows the thread out, and sails with the freed children and with Ariadne - whom he leaves sleeping on Naxos, where Dionysus finds her. He then forgets the sail, and Aegeus, watching from the cliff, sees black and throws himself into the sea that takes his name.

stories.title: Bellerophon and the Chimera
stories.summary: Falsely accused by the wife he refused, Bellerophon is sent to Lycia carrying a sealed message asking that the bearer be killed - the earliest such letter in Western literature, and one of the very few references to writing in Homer. King Iobates, unwilling to violate hospitality directly, sets him tasks meant to kill him, beginning with the Chimera, a fire-breathing composite of lion, goat and serpent. Athena has given Bellerophon a golden bridle in a dream, with which he catches and tames the winged horse Pegasus; from the air he is out of reach of the fire, and he kills the creature. Having survived every task, he is given half the kingdom. Then he tries to ride Pegasus up to Olympus as though he belonged there, and Zeus sends a gadfly; he falls, and ends alone, avoiding the paths of men.

stories.title: The Voyage of the Argo
stories.summary: Pelias, having usurped Iolcus, sends Jason for the Golden Fleece in Colchis expecting him not to return. Jason gathers the greatest crew in the tradition - Heracles, Orpheus, Castor and Polydeuces, and in some accounts Atalanta - and the Argo sails through the Clashing Rocks by releasing a dove first and rowing hard behind it. Aeetes sets three impossible conditions: yoke the fire-breathing bronze-hoofed bulls, sow the dragon's teeth and survive the armed men that spring up, and take the fleece from a serpent that never sleeps. His daughter Medea, in love with Jason, supplies the fireproof ointment, the trick of throwing a stone among the sown men so they kill each other, and the drug that puts the serpent to sleep. They escape, and Medea delays her father's pursuit by killing her own brother.

stories.title: Medea in Corinth
stories.summary: Settled in Corinth after their flight, Jason sets Medea aside to marry the king's daughter, arguing that the match secures a future for their sons. Medea, facing exile with nothing, is granted one day's grace. She sends her children to the bride with a gift of a robe and a golden diadem, which burn the princess to death and her father with her when he tries to hold her. Then she kills her own two sons - not in madness, but as the most complete injury available against a man whose entire future was that marriage and that line. Jason arrives to find them dead and Medea above him in a chariot sent by her grandfather Helios, refusing him even the bodies to bury. She goes to Athens; he dies years later, alone, struck by a beam from the rotting Argo.

stories.title: The Calydonian Boar Hunt
stories.summary: Oeneus of Calydon omits Artemis from a harvest sacrifice, and she sends a boar of enormous size to ravage the country. His son Meleager gathers the heroes of Greece to hunt it, and Atalanta comes with them, which several of the men object to. She draws first blood with an arrow; Meleager kills the animal and awards her the hide. His mother's brothers take it from her on the grounds that no woman should carry off the prize, and Meleager kills them both. His mother Althaea, hearing that her son has killed her brothers, takes from its chest the log on which his life depends, hidden there since his infancy, and puts it on the fire. He dies as it burns, and she kills herself afterwards.

stories.title: Orpheus and Eurydice
stories.summary: Eurydice dies of a snakebite on her wedding day, and Orpheus goes down after her. His singing does what no argument could: Charon ferries him living, Cerberus lies down, the wheel of Ixion stops, Tantalus forgets his thirst, and the Furies weep for the first time. Hades and Persephone agree to let her return on one condition - that he not look back at her until both are in the upper air. He walks the whole way up in silence, and within sight of daylight, unable to hear her footsteps and afraid she is not there, he turns. She is drawn back, and this time the way is closed. He refuses all company afterwards and is torn apart by Thracian women; his severed head floats down the river still singing.

stories.title: Oedipus at Thebes
stories.summary: Laius of Thebes, warned that his son will kill him, pins the infant's feet and exposes him; the child is rescued and raised in Corinth as a prince. Told by an oracle that he will kill his father and marry his mother, Oedipus leaves Corinth to protect the people he believes are his parents, and on the road kills a stranger in a quarrel at a crossroads. He answers the Sphinx's riddle, saves Thebes, and is given the throne and the widowed queen. Years later a plague forces an inquiry into the old king's unsolved murder, and the investigation - pressed hardest by Oedipus himself, against everyone urging him to stop - arrives at him. Jocasta hangs herself. He blinds himself with the pins of her brooches and goes into exile, led by his daughter.

stories.title: The Race of Atalanta
stories.summary: Pressed by her father to marry, Atalanta agrees only on terms: any suitor must beat her in a footrace, and those who lose are killed. She is the fastest runner in Greece and the heads of the losers accumulate. Hippomenes, watching, first thinks the prize cannot be worth it, then sees her run and asks Aphrodite for help. The goddess gives him three golden apples from her own grove. In the race he drops them one at a time, and Atalanta, who has no reason to stop and stops anyway, loses ground at each one and is beaten at the line. They marry, and afterwards forget to thank Aphrodite; she brings on them a desire so urgent that they lie together in a sanctuary, and are turned into lions for the sacrilege.

stories.title: The Judgement of Paris
stories.summary: Eris, not invited to the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, throws among the guests a golden apple inscribed to the fairest. Hera, Athena and Aphrodite each claim it. Zeus refuses to judge between his wife and his daughters and sends them to Mount Ida, where the Trojan prince Paris is herding cattle. Each offers a bribe: Hera power over Asia and Europe, Athena victory in every battle, Aphrodite the most beautiful woman in the world. Paris chooses Aphrodite. The woman is Helen, already married to Menelaus of Sparta, and her oath-bound suitors are obliged to recover her. So the largest story in Greek literature is set in motion by a wedding invitation, a comparison, and a young man asked to say which of three goddesses he prefers.

stories.title: The Sacrifice at Aulis
stories.summary: The fleet gathers at Aulis and cannot sail: the wind is dead against it, or there is no wind at all. Calchas reads the cause as the anger of Artemis, offended in most accounts because Agamemnon killed a deer in her grove and boasted, and declares that only the sacrifice of his daughter Iphigenia will free the fleet. Iphigenia is sent for on the pretext of a marriage to Achilles. Agamemnon does it. The wind comes, the fleet sails, and Clytemnestra is left with ten years to think about it - which is why he is killed in his bath on the day he comes home. In several versions Artemis substitutes a deer at the last moment and carries the girl away to Tauris to be her priestess, unknown to anyone present.

stories.title: The Wrath of Achilles
stories.summary: Apollo's priest comes to ransom his daughter from Agamemnon and is sent away insulted, and the god's arrows bring nine days of plague on the Greek camp. Calchas names the cause only after Achilles guarantees his safety. Agamemnon gives the girl back and takes Achilles' prize Briseis in her place, in public, to show who commands. Achilles withdraws from the fighting, and asks his mother Thetis to persuade Zeus to let the Greeks lose until they understand what he is worth. Zeus agrees. The rest of the poem is the working out of that request in full: the Greeks are driven back to their ships, embassies come with gifts, Achilles refuses, and the cost is finally paid by the person he loves most rather than by Agamemnon.

stories.title: Patroclus and Hector
stories.summary: With the Greeks driven back to the ships, Patroclus begs to be allowed to fight in Achilles' armour so the Trojans will think he has returned. Achilles agrees, on the condition that he drive them from the ships and come straight back. Patroclus does not come back; carried away, he pushes to the walls of Troy, and Apollo strikes the armour from him so that Euphorbus and then Hector can kill him. Achilles' grief converts directly into rage. Thetis brings him new armour made by Hephaestus, and he returns to the fighting, kills Hector before the walls, and then does what no one else in the poem does: lashes the body to his chariot and drags it round the tomb for days, refusing burial, until the gods themselves intervene.

stories.title: Priam in the Tent of Achilles
stories.summary: The gods will not allow Hector's body to be defiled further, and Zeus sends word to both sides. Guided by Hermes through the Greek lines at night, the old king Priam comes alone into the tent of the man who killed his son, kneels, and kisses the hands that did it, asking Achilles to remember his own father. Achilles, who has been unreachable for the whole poem, takes the old man's hand and pushes him gently away, and the two of them weep - Priam for Hector, Achilles for Patroclus and for Peleus, who will never see him again. He returns the body, agrees a truce of eleven days for the funeral, and the Iliad ends not with the fall of the city but with the burial of the man who defended it.

stories.title: The Wooden Horse
stories.summary: After ten years the city cannot be taken by force, so Odysseus proposes taking it by a gift. A great hollow horse is built, a picked company hides inside, and the Greek fleet withdraws behind the island of Tenedos, leaving one man to explain that the horse is an offering to Athena and deliberately too large to bring inside the walls. Cassandra says plainly that it holds armed men and is not believed, as she never is. The Trojans breach their own wall to bring it in and spend the night celebrating the end of the war. Helen is said to have walked around it calling to the men inside in the voices of their wives. At night the fleet returns, the company comes out, and the city is burned.

stories.title: The Return of Agamemnon
stories.summary: Clytemnestra has set a chain of beacon fires across the Aegean so that she will know the night Troy falls, and she is ready. Agamemnon arrives in triumph with Cassandra as his prize, and his wife greets him with a speech of welcome and spreads crimson cloth from his chariot to the door. It is a trap made of etiquette: to walk on it is the arrogance of an eastern king, and to refuse in front of the army is impossible. He walks on it. Inside, she kills him in the bath, wrapped in a robe he cannot get his arms out of, and Cassandra with him - having first stood outside and described the murder in detail to a chorus that hears her and does nothing. Clytemnestra comes out and tells them exactly what she has done, and why.

stories.title: The Cave of the Cyclops
stories.summary: Odysseus and twelve men enter a cave full of cheeses and penned lambs and wait to see who lives there, expecting the guest-gift that hospitality requires. What comes home is Polyphemus, who rolls a boulder across the entrance that no mortals could move, asks who they are, and answers the appeal to Zeus of strangers by eating two of them. Odysseus gives him strong unmixed wine, tells him his name is Nobody, and when the giant sleeps drives a sharpened olive stake into his single eye. The other Cyclopes, hearing him roar that Nobody is killing him, go away again. The men escape tied under the bellies of his rams. Then Odysseus, safely offshore, shouts his real name - and Polyphemus can pray to his father Poseidon by name, which costs him ten years.

stories.title: Circe on Aeaea
stories.summary: A scouting party finds a stone house in a clearing, with wolves and lions fawning around it and a woman singing at a great loom. She feeds them drugged food and touches them with her wand, and they become swine, penned and weeping, with their human minds intact. One man, who hung back, brings the news. Odysseus goes alone, and Hermes meets him on the way with the herb moly, which makes the drug useless; when Circe strikes him and nothing happens, she knows who he is, and he makes her swear a great oath not to harm him. She restores his men and becomes the most useful ally of the voyage, keeping them a year and then giving the sailing directions for everything that follows, including the instruction to go down to the dead first.

stories.title: The Book of the Dead
stories.summary: Following Circe's instructions, Odysseus sails to the edge of the world, digs a trench, and pours offerings of milk, honey, wine and water, then the blood of sacrificed sheep. The shades gather to it and he must hold them off with his sword until Tiresias has drunk and given his prophecy - the only shade Persephone allowed to keep his understanding. Afterwards he speaks with others: his mother, who died of grief for him and whom he cannot embrace; Agamemnon, who describes his own murder; Achilles, who says he would rather be a landless serf among the living than king over all the dead, which is the tradition's bleakest and most quoted statement about the afterlife; and Heracles, or his image, since the man himself is among the gods.

stories.title: The Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis
stories.summary: Circe's directions are precise and unforgiving. The Sirens must be passed with the crew's ears stopped with wax; if Odysseus wants to hear the song himself he must be lashed to the mast with orders to tighten the ropes when he begs. He hears it, and what they offer is not beauty but knowledge - they call him by name and promise to tell him everything that happened at Troy. Then the strait: Scylla on the cliff and Charybdis' whirlpool opposite, and no way through without loss. Circe tells him to hug the cliff and accept losing six men rather than risk the ship, and not to arm against her, because she is a deathless evil. He does as told. Watching her take them is the most pitiable thing, he says, that he saw in all his wanderings.

stories.title: The Bow and the Bed
stories.summary: Odysseus reaches Ithaca alone after twenty years and enters his own house disguised as a beggar, insulted by the suitors who have eaten his stores and courted his wife. Only his old nurse, washing his feet, knows him by a scar, and only his dying dog. Penelope, who has held them off for years by unpicking at night the shroud she wove by day, announces a contest: she will marry whoever can string her husband's bow and shoot through twelve axe-heads. No suitor can bend it. The beggar does, and turns it on them. Even then Penelope does not simply accept him; she orders their marriage bed carried out of the chamber, and when he objects that it cannot be moved because he built it around a living olive tree, she knows.

entities.name: Chaos
entities.role: The first thing that came to be
domains: the space in which things can exist
entities.bio: The void that existed first, from which Erebos and Night were born.
entities.longBio: Hesiod opens the Theogony by saying that Chaos came into being first of all, and after it broad-breasted Gaia, dim Tartaros and Eros. The word does not mean disorder in the modern sense; it comes from a root meaning to gape or yawn, and describes a gap or opening rather than a churning mess. Chaos is not a creator and does not act. Nothing is made by it and nothing is ruled by it; it simply is first, and from it Erebos and black Night are born, and from their union Aither and Day. Later writers, especially the Roman poets, reinterpreted the word toward the modern sense of a disordered mass of elements waiting to be sorted, and it is that Ovidian version, not the Hesiodic one, that most later European literature inherited. In cult Chaos has effectively no presence: there are no temples, no festivals and no images, which is consistent with its role as a starting condition rather than a god who can be approached.
entities.variantTraditions: Ovid's Metamorphoses recasts Chaos as a rude, undigested mass of warring elements separated by a god or kindlier nature, which is a Roman reworking rather than the Greek conception. Some Orphic theogonies begin instead with Chronos (Time) or with Nyx and a cosmic egg.

entities.name: Gaia
entities.role: The Earth herself, mother of the Titans
domains: the sure foundation of all things
festivals: Local Gaia cults at Athens, Olympia and Delphi, generally tied to oaths and to the dead
entities.worship: Worshipped less in grand temples than at oracular and oath-taking sites: she had a sanctuary and oracle at Delphi before Apollo in one tradition, an altar at Olympia, and a precinct at Athens. Offerings were often poured into the ground rather than burned upward, in the manner used for chthonic powers.
entities.bio: The earth as a living being, who bore Ouranos and then the Titans by him, and who drove two dynastic overthrows.
entities.longBio: Gaia comes into being immediately after Chaos as the sure foundation of everything, and she is the most consequential actor in the early Theogony. She produces Ouranos the starry sky by herself, along with the mountains and Pontos the sea, and then bears the twelve Titans, the Cyclopes and the Hundred-Handers to Ouranos. When Ouranos pushes his children back inside her so that none can be born, it is Gaia who makes the adamant sickle and finds in Cronus a son willing to use it. She repeats the pattern a generation later, warning Rhea how to save Zeus and later advising Zeus how to win the Titanomachy, then turning against him too and bearing Typhon to challenge him. Her oracle at Delphi is older than Apollo's in the tradition Aeschylus reports, and she is invoked in oaths precisely because the earth is what cannot be evaded.
entities.variantTraditions: Aeschylus in the Eumenides makes Gaia the first holder of the Delphic oracle, passed to Themis, then Phoebe, then Apollo; other accounts have Apollo seize it by killing Python. Roman writers identify her with Terra or Tellus Mater.

entities.name: Ouranos
entities.role: The starry sky; first ruler of the cosmos
domains: the heavens as a physical covering
entities.bio: The sky, born of Gaia and then her consort, castrated by his son Cronus and displaced.
entities.longBio: Gaia bore Ouranos equal to herself, to cover her about and be an everlasting home for the gods, and then bore the Titans to him. Ouranos hated his children from the first and hid each one away inside Gaia rather than let it come to the light, so that the earth groaned with being overfull. Gaia forged a sickle of grey adamant and asked her sons to act; only Cronus, the youngest, took it up. He cut off his father's genitals from ambush and threw them behind him: from the drops of blood that fell on the earth came the Erinyes, the Giants and the Meliae, and from the foam gathered about the severed flesh in the sea came Aphrodite. Ouranos survives the mutilation but ceases to rule or to father, and he passes out of the narrative except to give the prophecy, with Gaia, that Cronus would in his turn be overcome by his own son.
entities.variantTraditions: Some later accounts soften or omit the castration. Roman writers call him Caelus. Orphic theogonies place different figures at the head of the succession, with Phanes or Chronos preceding the sky.

entities.name: Nyx
entities.role: Night, born of Chaos
entities.abode: A house in the depths, beyond Tartaros, which she shares with Day but never enters at the same time
entities.bio: Night herself, mother of Sleep, Death, the Fates and a long line of grim powers.
entities.longBio: Nyx is born from Chaos and is one of the very few beings the Theogony treats as genuinely awesome to the other gods. She bears Aither and Day to Erebos, and then, without any father, produces a catalogue of abstractions that shape mortal life: Doom, Fate, Death, Sleep, Blame, Distress, the Hesperides, the Moirai, Nemesis, Deceit, Old Age and Strife. She lives in a house at the edge of things where she and Day greet one another on the threshold as one goes out and the other comes in, so that the house never holds both. Homer preserves a striking detail of her standing: in the Iliad, Zeus is furious with Hypnos for a trick but holds back from striking him because Hypnos fled to Nyx for refuge, and Zeus shrank from doing anything displeasing to swift Night. She is rarely worshipped and rarely depicted, and functions in the tradition as a source of powers rather than a personality.
entities.variantTraditions: Orphic tradition promotes Nyx considerably, making her a primary cosmic principle and an oracular power who advises Zeus, in some versions preceding even Chaos as the origin of things.

entities.name: Erebos
entities.role: Primordial darkness
domains: the dark passage of the dead
entities.abode: Between the earth and the house of Hades
entities.bio: The darkness born of Chaos, who fathered Aither and Day upon his sister Night.
entities.longBio: Erebos is born from Chaos alongside Nyx, and the two produce their opposites: Aither, the bright upper air the gods breathe, and Hemera, Day. Beyond that genealogy he barely acts. His name is used far more often as a place than as a person, standing for the dark region the dead pass through on their way to the house of Hades, so that Homer and later poets say a man has gone to Erebos in the way we would say he has gone to the grave. The pairing of Erebos and Nyx producing Aither and Day is one of the clearest expressions of a pattern that runs through the early Theogony, in which the first beings generate their own opposites rather than a graded series of similar things.
entities.variantTraditions: Some accounts make Erebos rather than Chaos the immediate origin of further beings; Roman writers often use Erebus simply as a name for the underworld as a whole.

entities.name: Tartaros
entities.role: The pit below the underworld
epithets: As Far Below Hades As Heaven Is Above Earth
entities.bio: Both a primordial being and the pit where defeated powers are confined.
entities.longBio: Hesiod names dim Tartaros among the very first beings, alongside Gaia and Eros, and then uses the same name for a place. As a location it is measured with a memorable image: an anvil falling from heaven would take nine days to reach the earth, and nine more from earth to reach Tartaros, which is fenced with bronze and ringed three times over by night. It is where Ouranos confined the Hundred-Handers and Cyclopes, where Zeus casts the defeated Titans under the guard of those same Hundred-Handers, and where Typhon is hurled after his defeat. As a being, Tartaros fathers Typhon upon Gaia, which is the one moment the personified sense is unavoidable. Later, especially in Plato and in Roman poetry, Tartaros becomes specifically the place of punishment for the wicked, distinct from the neutral house of Hades, and it is this moralised version that passes into later European use.
entities.variantTraditions: In Homer, Tartaros is essentially the prison of the Titans rather than a place of punishment for mortals; the moralised sense grows later, and Virgil's Aeneid VI gives the fullest developed description.

entities.name: Eros (Primordial)
entities.role: Desire, the force that joins
domains: the impulse that makes beings unite
entities.bio: The primordial force of attraction, named among the first beings, distinct from the later winged boy.
entities.longBio: Hesiod names Eros immediately after Chaos, Gaia and Tartaros, calling him fairest among the deathless gods, the loosener of limbs, who overcomes the reason and careful planning of all gods and all men. This Eros is not a character with a story; he is the principle that makes the successive generations of the Theogony possible at all, since without attraction the pairings that produce sky, sea, Titans and gods would not occur. He is quite distinct from the familiar Eros who is the son of Aphrodite, a mischievous archer whose arrows cause specific infatuations, and who belongs to a much later and more literary phase of the tradition. The Greeks themselves noticed the difference: Plato has speakers in the Symposium argue over whether Eros is among the oldest of gods or one of the youngest, precisely because both traditions were current.
entities.variantTraditions: The later Eros is the son of Aphrodite, variously by Ares, Hermes or Zeus, and is the model for the Roman Cupid. Orphic theogonies identify the primordial Eros with Phanes, the shining first-born who emerges from the cosmic egg.

entities.name: Pontos
entities.role: The sea, born of Gaia alone
entities.bio: The sea as a primordial being, father of the old sea-gods before Poseidon.
entities.longBio: Gaia bears Pontos without any partner, as she bears the mountains and Ouranos, and he stands for the sea as a raw fact rather than as a domain someone rules. With Gaia he fathers the older generation of sea powers: Nereus, called the Old Man of the Sea and famed for never lying; Thaumas, father of Iris and the Harpies; Phorcys and Ceto, whose children are the Gorgons, the Graeae and other monsters of the deep; and Eurybia. This line matters because it shows the sea being populated well before Poseidon, an Olympian who acquires the sea by lot rather than by descent. The older sea powers are generally shape-shifting, prophetic and truthful, and they persist alongside the Olympians rather than being overthrown, which is unusual in a tradition otherwise organised around succession by conquest.
entities.variantTraditions: Later writers often collapse Pontos into Oceanus or simply into Poseidon's domain; Roman poets use Pontus mainly as a poetic word for the sea.

entities.name: Cronus
entities.role: Titan king; god of time's harvest
entities.abode: Mount Othrys during his reign; afterwards Tartaros, or in another tradition the Isles of the Blest
festivals: Kronia at Athens, a midsummer harvest festival at which masters and slaves ate together
entities.worship: Worship of Cronus was thin in classical Greece and deliberately old-fashioned in flavour. The Athenian Kronia inverted normal order for a day, with slaves feasting alongside masters, in memory of the age when no one served anyone. He had a sanctuary at Olympia on the hill named for him.
entities.bio: The Titan who castrated his father and swallowed his children, and was overthrown by Zeus.
entities.longBio: Cronus is the youngest of the twelve Titans and the only one willing to take up Gaia's sickle against Ouranos. Having taken the throne, he inherits his father's fear: warned by Gaia and Ouranos that his own son would overcome him, he swallows each child Rhea bears as soon as it is born. Rhea, pregnant with Zeus, appeals to her parents, gives birth in secret on Crete and hands Cronus a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes, which he swallows believing it is the child. Grown, Zeus forces him to disgorge first the stone and then his brothers and sisters, and the ten-year Titanomachy follows, ending with the Titans confined in Tartaros. A quite different strand of tradition, visible in Hesiod's own Works and Days and strong in the Roman Saturn, remembers Cronus as the king of the Golden Age, when men lived without toil, and gives him a peaceful retirement ruling the Isles of the Blest.
entities.variantTraditions: The Golden Age Cronus and the child-swallowing Cronus sit awkwardly together and were reconciled in different ways by different writers. The Romans identified him with Saturn, whose December festival, the Saturnalia, preserved the Golden Age association. The similarity of his name to Chronos, Time, is a later etymological play rather than an original identity.

entities.name: Rhea
entities.role: Titan queen; mother of the first Olympians
entities.worship: Rhea's cult is largely absorbed into that of the Great Mother, with ecstatic rites, drums and lions, strongest in Crete and Asia Minor and imported to Rome as Magna Mater in 204 BCE.
entities.bio: Sister and consort of Cronus, who saved Zeus by substituting a stone.
entities.longBio: Rhea bears Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, Poseidon and Zeus to Cronus, and watches him swallow each one. Pregnant with her last child, she goes to Gaia and Ouranos for counsel and is sent to Lyctus on Crete, where she bears Zeus by night and gives him to Gaia to hide in a cave on Mount Aegaeon or Ida. To Cronus she gives a great stone wrapped in swaddling bands, which he takes for the child and swallows. The infant Zeus is nursed in the cave, in the common version by the goat Amaltheia and guarded by the Kouretes, young armed men who clash their shields so that his crying cannot be heard. Rhea's decisive act is the hinge of the whole succession sequence, and she is one of the few figures to appear on the winning side of a generational change without being of that generation.
entities.variantTraditions: Rhea is widely identified with the Anatolian Great Mother Cybele, and by the Romans with Ops and with Magna Mater; the Cretan details of the birth cave vary between Ida and Dicte in different sources.

entities.name: Oceanus
entities.role: Titan of the world-encircling river
domains: the river that rings the world
symbols: the bull's horns of a river-god
entities.abode: The river Oceanus at the edge of the world
entities.bio: The eldest Titan, the great river encircling the earth, father of the rivers and the Oceanids.
entities.longBio: Oceanus is the eldest of the Titans and, with his sister Tethys, the parent of some three thousand rivers and three thousand Oceanid nymphs, a number Hesiod gives as a way of saying they cannot be counted. He is conceived not as a sea but as a vast fresh-water river running in a circle around the flat earth, from which all other waters flow and to which they return. Alone among the Titans he takes no part in the Titanomachy, and in consequence is not confined to Tartaros; he stays at the edge of the world, unaligned. Homer at one point calls Oceanus and Tethys the origin of the gods, a phrase later writers seized on as evidence of an older water-cosmogony behind the Hesiodic one. In the Prometheus Bound he appears as a cautious elder who flies in on a winged creature to advise Prometheus to moderate his defiance, and is dismissed for it.
entities.variantTraditions: The Homeric line making Oceanus and Tethys the origin of the gods conflicts with Hesiod's genealogy and was much discussed in antiquity; Plato cites it in the Theaetetus as an ancient doctrine that all things flow.

entities.name: Tethys
entities.role: Titan of nursing waters
entities.abode: The river Oceanus at the edge of the world
entities.bio: Sister and consort of Oceanus, mother of the rivers and the Oceanids.
entities.longBio: Tethys bears the rivers, the springs and the Oceanid nymphs to Oceanus, and her role in the tradition is overwhelmingly that of a source and a nurse rather than an actor. Her one substantial appearance in Homer is in a scene where Hera claims to be going to the ends of the earth to visit Oceanus and Tethys, who reared her when Zeus was overthrowing Cronus, which places Tethys as a foster-mother to an Olympian during the war. She takes no part in the Titanomachy. In a story preserved by Ovid she is asked by Hera to punish Callisto, set in the sky as the Great Bear, by forbidding her the privilege of bathing in the ocean, which is the mythological explanation for why that constellation never sets below the horizon in Greek latitudes.
entities.variantTraditions: Tethys is frequently confused in later use with Thetis, the sea-nymph mother of Achilles, who is an entirely different figure; the two names are distinct in Greek.

entities.name: Hyperion
entities.role: Titan of heavenly light
domains: the ordered course of the heavenly bodies
entities.bio: Titan father of the Sun, Moon and Dawn.
entities.longBio: Hyperion is one of the twelve Titans and, with his sister Theia, the father of Helios the Sun, Selene the Moon and Eos the Dawn. His name means the one who goes above, and it is used in Homer as an epithet of the Sun himself, so that Helios Hyperion can be read either as Helios son of Hyperion or as Helios the one who travels on high. He has no narrative of his own, which is typical of the second rank of Titans: they exist chiefly to father the powers that do act. He is named among the Titans who joined Cronus in ambushing Ouranos, holding one corner of the sky while Cronus struck, and is confined with the rest after the Titanomachy.
entities.variantTraditions: Because Homer uses Hyperion as an epithet of the Sun, some later sources treat Hyperion and Helios as the same figure rather than father and son.

entities.name: Theia
entities.role: Titan of sight and shining
domains: the gleam of gold and silver
entities.bio: Titan mother of Helios, Selene and Eos, associated with sight and the gleam of precious metal.
entities.longBio: Theia bears the Sun, the Moon and the Dawn to her brother Hyperion. Pindar preserves an unusual and revealing detail about her: he addresses her as the mother of the sun and says that it is because of her that men value gold and prize it above other possessions, connecting her not merely to light but to the human perception of brightness as worth. The Greeks held a theory of vision in which the eye emits a beam, and Theia sits behind that idea as the power that makes seeing possible. Like most of the female Titans she takes no part in the war and has no cult of consequence, but the association of shining, sight and value gives her a more distinct character than the other Titanesses of her rank.
entities.variantTraditions: She is also called Euryphaessa, wide-shining, in the Homeric Hymn to Helios, where that name appears in place of Theia for the Sun's mother.

entities.name: Coeus
entities.role: Titan of the northern pillar and of enquiry
entities.bio: Titan father of Leto and Asteria; associated with the north and with enquiry.
entities.longBio: Coeus is one of the four brothers who, in Apollodorus' account, held down the corners of the sky while Cronus struck at Ouranos, and he is assigned the north. With his sister Phoebe he fathers Leto, who bears Apollo and Artemis to Zeus, and Asteria, who bears Hecate. That makes him grandfather to two of the most prominent Olympians and to the most independent of the goddesses, which is his main significance in the tradition. His name was connected in antiquity with the word for questioning or enquiry, and also with polos, the axis or pole of the sky, and both associations sit comfortably with a Titan of the north and of intelligence. He fought against Zeus and was confined in Tartaros.
entities.variantTraditions: Roman writers call him Polus. Valerius Flaccus gives a scene of Coeus breaking his chains in Tartaros and being subdued again, which has no Greek precedent.

entities.name: Phoebe
entities.role: Titan of prophetic brightness
entities.bio: Titan holder of the Delphic oracle, who passed it to her grandson Apollo.
entities.longBio: Phoebe bears Leto and Asteria to Coeus. Her importance is concentrated in a single tradition, given by Aeschylus at the opening of the Eumenides, in which the Delphic oracle passes down a female line by gift rather than by force: from Gaia to Themis, from Themis to Phoebe, and from Phoebe to Apollo as a birthday gift, so that Apollo takes the name Phoebus from her. This lineage matters because it presents the most authoritative oracle in Greece as an orderly inheritance rather than a conquest, in deliberate contrast to the alternative tradition in which Apollo takes Delphi by killing the serpent Python. Phoebe herself gives no oracles in any surviving narrative, and like the other Titanesses she is absent from the war.
entities.variantTraditions: The competing tradition, in the Homeric Hymn to Apollo and elsewhere, has Apollo seize Delphi by slaying Python, with no mention of an inheritance from Phoebe.

entities.name: Crius
entities.role: Titan of the south; the ram
entities.bio: Titan of the southern quarter, father of Astraeus, Pallas and Perses.
entities.longBio: Crius is the least developed of the twelve Titans. He holds the southern corner of the sky in the ambush of Ouranos, and by Eurybia, daughter of Gaia and Pontos, he fathers Astraeus, father of the winds and stars; Pallas, father of Nike, Kratos, Bia and Zelos; and Perses, father of Hecate. He has no narrative and no cult. His name is the ordinary Greek word for ram, and later writers connected him with the constellation Aries, though this looks like an etymological inference rather than an inherited tradition. He fought with the Titans and was confined in Tartaros with them.
entities.variantTraditions: Some sources omit Crius from the twelve Titans entirely, substituting another name; his children are more prominent in the tradition than he is.

entities.name: Iapetus
entities.role: Titan ancestor of humankind
entities.bio: Titan father of Prometheus, Epimetheus, Atlas and Menoetius.
entities.longBio: Iapetus holds the west in the ambush of Ouranos, and by the Oceanid Clymene he fathers four sons whose careers between them define the relationship of gods and men: Atlas, condemned to hold up the sky; Menoetius, struck down by Zeus for insolence; Prometheus, who steals fire and is punished for it; and Epimetheus, who accepts Pandora. Because Prometheus is credited in many accounts with making the first humans, and because all four sons are marked by overreach and its consequences, Iapetus came to be regarded as an ancestor of mortals and as a figure associated with the human condition. He himself does nothing beyond fathering them, and is confined in Tartaros after the war.
entities.variantTraditions: Iapetus was compared in antiquity and by later scholars with the biblical Japheth, though the connection is speculative. Some sources give his wife as Asia rather than Clymene.

entities.name: Themis
entities.role: Titan of divine law and right order
entities.abode: Olympus, at the side of Zeus
entities.worship: Themis had altars and temples at Athens, Olympia and Delphi, and was invoked at the opening of assemblies and in matters of oath and hospitality.
entities.bio: Titan of established custom and right order, oracular predecessor at Delphi, and counsellor to Zeus.
entities.longBio: Themis is a Titan who ends up on the winning side and stays there. She holds the Delphic oracle after Gaia and before Phoebe in Aeschylus' account, and she becomes the second wife of Zeus, bearing the Horai, the seasons, and the Moirai, the Fates, in one common genealogy. Her domain is not law in the sense of legislation but the settled order of what is right and customary, which is why she presides over assemblies: it is Themis who calls the gods to council in the Iliad. She also has a strong prophetic aspect. In the Prometheus Bound, Aeschylus identifies her with Gaia and makes her the source of Prometheus' fatal knowledge about the marriage that would produce a son greater than his father, the secret that gives Prometheus leverage over Zeus. Her placement beside Zeus, advising rather than opposing, marks her as the point where the older order is absorbed rather than defeated.
entities.variantTraditions: Hesiod makes the Moirai daughters of Zeus and Themis in one passage and daughters of Nyx alone in another, an inconsistency the tradition never resolved. The Roman Justitia inherits her scales and becomes the modern figure of Justice.

entities.name: Mnemosyne
entities.role: Titan of memory, mother of the Muses
entities.bio: Titan of memory, who bore the nine Muses to Zeus on nine successive nights.
entities.longBio: Mnemosyne is memory itself, and in a culture whose poetry was composed and transmitted orally that makes her foundational rather than decorative. Hesiod says Zeus lay with her for nine nights in Pieria and that she bore the nine Muses, who are invoked at the opening of epic precisely because the poet needs to be given what he cannot know first-hand. The Theogony's own proem is addressed to them. Beyond that genealogy she is barely a character. She acquires a further role in the mystery traditions: gold leaves buried with initiates in southern Italy and Crete instruct the dead to avoid the spring of Lethe, forgetfulness, and to drink instead from the pool of Mnemosyne, so that memory rather than oblivion becomes the mark of a soul that has escaped the ordinary round.
entities.variantTraditions: The number and names of the Muses vary in earlier sources; some traditions give three Muses rather than nine, and Pausanias records both.

entities.name: Prometheus
entities.role: The Titan who stole fire for humankind
entities.abode: Bound to a crag in the Caucasus; afterwards free
festivals: Prometheia at Athens, with a torch race run from his altar in the Academy
entities.worship: Prometheus was honoured at Athens alongside Hephaestus and Athena as a patron of craftsmen, with an altar in the Academy from which torch races were run into the city.
entities.bio: The Titan who tricked Zeus, stole fire in a fennel stalk, and was bound to a rock for it.
entities.longBio: Prometheus, son of Iapetus, sides with Zeus in the Titanomachy but then twice takes the mortals' part against him. At Mecone he divides a sacrificial ox into two portions, hiding the meat under the ugly stomach and the bare bones under glistening fat, and invites Zeus to choose; Zeus takes the fat and the bones, and thereafter men keep the meat and burn the bones for the gods. In return Zeus withholds fire from mortals, and Prometheus steals it back in a hollow fennel stalk. His punishment is to be bound to a crag where an eagle eats his liver each day, the liver growing back each night, until Heracles shoots the eagle generations later. In Aeschylus he is given a further dimension: he knows a secret, that a particular marriage would produce a son greater than his father, and he refuses to tell it, so that his defiance is not merely theft but leverage. Aeschylus also credits him with giving mortals not just fire but number, writing, medicine and navigation.
entities.variantTraditions: In several sources, including Ovid and Pausanias, Prometheus also creates the first humans out of clay. Hesiod does not say this. The reconciliation with Zeus, in which the secret is finally told, came in Aeschylus' lost sequel Prometheus Unbound.

entities.name: Atlas
entities.role: The Titan who holds up the sky
entities.abode: The far west, at the edge of the world
entities.bio: Condemned after the Titanomachy to hold the sky apart from the earth for ever.
entities.longBio: Atlas, son of Iapetus, leads the Titans in the war and receives a punishment shaped to fit a leader: not confinement in Tartaros with the rest, but the endless labour of standing at the western edge of the world holding up the sky, keeping heaven and earth apart so that the arrangement Cronus overturned cannot recur. He is father of the Pleiades, the Hyades and, in most accounts, of Calypso. Two heroes meet him. Heracles, sent for the apples of the Hesperides, offers to take the burden while Atlas fetches them; Atlas returns and proposes to leave Heracles holding it permanently, and is tricked into taking it back for a moment while Heracles adjusts a pad on his shoulders. Perseus, refused hospitality, shows him the Gorgon's head and turns him to stone, which is offered as the origin of the Atlas mountains.
entities.variantTraditions: The two stories are inconsistent, since Atlas cannot both be turned to stone by Perseus and later meet Heracles; ancient writers noticed and generally kept them apart. Later allegorists made him an astronomer king of Mauretania, which is how his name came to be attached to books of maps.

entities.name: Epimetheus
entities.role: Afterthought; the brother who accepted Pandora
epithets: The One Who Learns Too Late
entities.bio: The brother of Prometheus, who accepted Zeus' gift of Pandora against warning.
entities.longBio: Epimetheus is defined entirely by contrast with his brother: where Prometheus is forethought, Epimetheus is the one who understands afterwards. Prometheus warns him never to accept a gift from Zeus and to send it straight back; Epimetheus takes Pandora anyway, and only realises the harm once it is done. Plato, in the Protagoras, gives a fuller version in which the two brothers are set to equip the newly made creatures, and Epimetheus asks to do the distributing himself. He gives out the available qualities - speed, claws, thick hides, wings - so freely to the animals that when he reaches humankind nothing is left, which is why Prometheus must then steal fire and craft to make good the shortfall. Epimetheus and Pandora have a daughter, Pyrrha, who with Deucalion survives the flood and repopulates the earth.
entities.variantTraditions: Hesiod's Works and Days and Theogony give slightly different accounts of Pandora's arrival; Plato's distribution story is a philosophical elaboration rather than an inherited myth.

entities.name: Helios
entities.role: The Sun, who sees and hears everything
epithets: He Who Gives Light to Mortals and Immortals
entities.abode: A palace in the east; he returns each night by the stream of Oceanus
festivals: Halieia at Rhodes, with games and the sacrifice of a chariot team driven into the sea
entities.worship: Helios' major cult was on Rhodes, where he was the chief god of the island and honoured with the Halieia; elsewhere he was more often invoked in oaths and curses than given temples.
entities.bio: The Sun, who drives his chariot across the sky daily and witnesses everything that happens.
entities.longBio: Helios, son of Hyperion and Theia, drives a chariot drawn by four horses from east to west each day and returns overnight in a golden cup floating on Oceanus. Because he sees everything, he functions in the tradition as a witness: it is Helios who tells Demeter that Hades has taken Persephone, and Helios who informs Hephaestus of Aphrodite's affair with Ares. Oaths are sworn by him for the same reason. His cattle graze on the island of Thrinacia, and when Odysseus' starving crew kill them he demands redress from Zeus and threatens to shine among the dead instead, which brings the thunderbolt that destroys the ship. His son Phaethon begs to drive the chariot for a day, loses control, scorches the earth and is struck down by Zeus. From the classical period onward Helios is increasingly identified with Apollo, though Homer and Hesiod keep them entirely distinct.
entities.variantTraditions: The identification of Helios with Apollo is a later development, common by the fifth century BCE and standard in Roman poetry, but absent from the earliest sources. Rhodes maintained an independent and vigorous cult of Helios, whose colossal statue stood at its harbour.

entities.name: Selene
entities.role: The Moon
entities.abode: The night sky; the cave of Latmos in the story of Endymion
entities.bio: The Moon, sister of the Sun, who loved the sleeping shepherd Endymion.
entities.longBio: Selene, daughter of Hyperion and Theia, drives a chariot drawn by two horses across the night sky, wearing the crescent as a crown. Her best-known story concerns Endymion, a young shepherd or king of Elis with whom she falls in love; at her request, or by Zeus' decision, he is given eternal sleep and unfading youth in a cave on Mount Latmos, where she visits him, and she bears him fifty daughters. She is one of three moon-associated figures, alongside Artemis and Hecate, who are increasingly conflated from the classical period on, though in the early tradition Selene alone is the moon as a body. Her month-marking function gave her a role in ordinary reckoning that the mythology hardly reflects.
entities.variantTraditions: By the Hellenistic period Selene, Artemis and Hecate are often treated as three aspects of one goddess, an identification the Romans continued with Luna and Diana. The Endymion story is told with several different explanations for the sleep.

entities.name: Eos
entities.role: The Dawn
entities.abode: The eastern edge of the world, by the stream of Oceanus
entities.bio: The Dawn, who rises each morning and repeatedly carries off mortal youths.
entities.longBio: Eos, sister of Helios and Selene, rises from Oceanus each morning to bring light, and is given the standing epithet rosy-fingered in Homer. With Astraeus she bears the winds and the morning star. She is notorious for abducting handsome mortals, a pattern the tradition explains as a curse laid on her by Aphrodite for sleeping with Ares. Her most consequential victim is Tithonus, for whom she asks Zeus for immortality but forgets to ask for unending youth, so that he shrivels into extreme old age, babbling endlessly, and is finally shut away or turned into a cicada. Their son Memnon, king of the Ethiopians, is killed by Achilles at Troy, and Eos' grief for him is one of the more affecting scenes in the epic cycle; the morning dew was explained as her tears.
entities.variantTraditions: The Roman Aurora inherits her role directly. The Tithonus story is told in the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite as a warning about the mismatch between gods and mortals.

entities.name: Leto
entities.role: Mother of Apollo and Artemis
entities.worship: Leto was honoured principally alongside Apollo and Artemis, most substantially at the Letoon in Lycia and on Delos, where her cult was inseparable from her son's.
entities.bio: Titan daughter of Coeus and Phoebe, who bore Apollo and Artemis on Delos after long persecution by Hera.
entities.longBio: Leto, pregnant by Zeus, is refused a place to give birth by every land on earth, in most accounts because Hera has forbidden it or because the lands fear Hera's anger. Only Delos, a small floating island of no consequence, agrees, on the condition that Apollo will honour it with his temple; the island is thereafter anchored. Even there the birth is delayed, because Hera detains Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth, until the other goddesses bribe her with a great necklace. Artemis is born first and, in a detail the tradition enjoys, assists at the birth of her brother. Leto's later appearances are chiefly as a mother defended by her children: when Niobe boasts of having many children where Leto has only two, Apollo and Artemis shoot every one of Niobe's; when the giant Tityos assaults her, they kill him.
entities.variantTraditions: Some accounts have Artemis born on Ortygia rather than Delos. Leto had an important independent cult in Lycia, where a major sanctuary, the Letoon, was shared with her children.

entities.name: Asteria
entities.role: Titan of the falling stars and of night oracles
entities.abode: The island of Delos, which the tradition identifies with her
entities.bio: Titan sister of Leto, who became the island of Delos to escape Zeus.
entities.longBio: Asteria, daughter of Coeus and Phoebe, bears Hecate to Perses, which makes her the mother of the goddess of crossroads and witchcraft. Her own story is one of escape: pursued by Zeus, she turns herself into a quail and flings herself into the sea, becoming a floating island. That island is identified with Delos, so that the place which alone will receive her sister Leto in labour is Asteria herself, a connection the Homeric Hymn to Apollo and Callimachus both draw out. She is among the very few figures in the tradition to evade Zeus successfully, at the cost of ceasing to be a person. Her associations with night, stars and prophetic dreams are attested but thin.
entities.variantTraditions: Callimachus' Hymn to Delos develops the identification of Asteria with the island most fully; older sources sometimes keep the island and the Titaness separate.

entities.name: Zeus
entities.role: King of the gods; sky, thunder and oaths
festivals: Olympic Games at Olympia, every four years
entities.worship: The most widely worshipped god in the Greek world, with the great sanctuary and gold-and-ivory statue at Olympia, the oracle of the rustling oaks at Dodona, and altars in every city. Sacrifice was normally burnt upward, the standard rite for the sky gods.
entities.bio: Youngest son of Cronus, who overthrew his father and rules the gods as king.
entities.longBio: Zeus is saved at birth by Rhea's substitution of a stone, raised in secret on Crete, and returns to force Cronus to disgorge his swallowed brothers and sisters. He frees the Cyclopes, who give him the thunderbolt, and the Hundred-Handers, whose hurled rocks decide the ten-year Titanomachy. Afterwards the three brothers draw lots: Zeus takes the sky, Poseidon the sea, Hades the world below, and the earth and Olympus are held in common.
