His rule is not absolute in the way a creator's would be. He is bound by oaths sworn on the Styx, constrained by Fate, and repeatedly outmanoeuvred by Hera. What he does hold absolutely is the enforcement of two obligations the Greeks regarded as the floor of civilisation: the oath and the guest-host bond, which is why his two most invoked titles are Horkios and Xenios. His many unions with goddesses and mortal women are less romance than genealogy, producing most of the second-rank gods and nearly every major hero, and they are the engine of Hera's persistent hostility.
entities.variantTraditions: Zeus swallows his first wife Metis when warned that her son would surpass him, which is why Athena is born from his head - the succession pattern of Ouranos and Cronus broken only by being anticipated. Cretan tradition uncomfortably showed a tomb of Zeus, which other Greeks cited as proof that Cretans were liars.

entities.name: Hera
entities.role: Queen of the gods; marriage and legitimate succession
entities.abode: Mount Olympus; her great temples at Argos and Samos
festivals: Heraia at Argos and Olympia, including footraces for unmarried women
entities.worship: Among the oldest Greek cults, with monumental temples at Argos, Samos, Olympia and Paestum. Brides and married women were her particular constituency, and the Heraia at Olympia gave women their own games.
entities.bio: Sister and wife of Zeus, guardian of marriage, and implacable enemy of his children by other women.
entities.longBio: Hera is swallowed by Cronus and disgorged with the rest, and becomes Zeus' wife after a courtship in which he takes the form of a bedraggled cuckoo to reach her. Her domain is marriage as an institution rather than love, which explains a character often misread as mere jealousy: what she pursues is the standing of the legitimate wife and the legitimate line. Her campaigns are formidable and long. She delays the birth of Heracles so that Eurystheus is born first and Heracles must serve him, sends serpents to his cradle, and drives him mad. She hounds Leto across the earth to prevent Apollo and Artemis being born, torments Io and Semele, and takes the Greek side at Troy with unrelenting energy because a Trojan judged Aphrodite fairer than her. She is also capable of directly opposing Zeus: in the Iliad she seduces and drugs him to sleep so the Greeks can advance, and she once joins a plot to bind him.
entities.variantTraditions: Her cult at Argos and Samos is older and grander than her mythological role suggests, and some scholars read her as a pre-Greek great goddess absorbed into the Olympian family as a wife. The Romans identified her with Juno.

entities.name: Poseidon
entities.role: Lord of the sea, earthquakes and horses
entities.abode: A palace in the depths off Aegae; Olympus when he attends
festivals: Isthmian Games near Corinth, every two years
entities.worship: Major sanctuaries at Sounion, Isthmia and Helike. Sailors sacrificed to him before voyages, and horses and bulls were his characteristic victims.
entities.bio: Zeus' brother, who drew the sea by lot; a violent and easily slighted power.
entities.longBio: Poseidon receives the sea when the three brothers divide the cosmos, though the older sea powers descended from Pontos are already there and he never fully displaces them. He is the Earth-Shaker: the Greeks attributed earthquakes to the striking of his trident, which makes him a god of the land's instability as much as the water. He created the horse, or produced the first one by striking a rock, and horses are sacrificed to him by drowning. His temper drives much of his mythology. Losing the contest for Athens to Athena, whose olive was judged more useful than his salt spring, he floods the plain. Slighted by Laomedon over unpaid wages for building Troy's walls, he sends a sea monster and later fights for the Greeks. Most consequentially, after Odysseus blinds his son Polyphemus, he keeps him from home for ten years, which is the whole engine of the Odyssey.
entities.variantTraditions: In Arcadia and Boeotia, Poseidon's oldest cults are of a freshwater and horse god with no maritime element, which suggests the sea rulership was acquired rather than original. The Romans identified him with Neptune.

entities.name: Demeter
entities.role: Goddess of grain, agriculture and the Mysteries
domains: the cycle of the growing year
entities.abode: Olympus; and Eleusis, where she was received in her grief
entities.worship: The Eleusinian Mysteries ran for roughly two millennia and promised initiates a better lot after death; their content was protected by an oath of silence that was, remarkably, kept. The Thesmophoria was celebrated by married women across the Greek world.
entities.bio: Goddess of grain, whose search for her stolen daughter explains the seasons and founded the Eleusinian Mysteries.
entities.longBio: When Hades carries off Persephone with Zeus' consent, Demeter searches the earth for nine days by torchlight, learns the truth from Helios, and withdraws from Olympus in fury. Disguised as an old woman she comes to Eleusis, is taken in by the royal house, and nurses the prince Demophoon, whom she secretly holds in the fire each night to burn away his mortality until his mother sees and screams. Revealing herself, she demands a temple. Then she stops the grain: nothing grows, and mankind faces extinction while the gods face the loss of sacrifice. Zeus is forced to negotiate. Persephone is returned, but because she has eaten pomegranate seeds in the underworld she must spend part of each year below, and Demeter's grief in those months is the barren season. Before departing she teaches the Eleusinians her rites, which became the most revered mystery cult in the Greek world.
entities.variantTraditions: The number of pomegranate seeds and the length of Persephone's absence vary between sources - four months in the Homeric Hymn, six in later accounts. The Romans identified Demeter with Ceres.

entities.name: Athena
entities.role: Goddess of wisdom, craft and strategic war
symbols: the aegis with the Gorgon's head
festivals: Panathenaia at Athens, annually and with a Great Panathenaia every four years
entities.worship: The Parthenon housed her gold-and-ivory statue, and the Great Panathenaia carried a newly woven robe to her ancient olive-wood image. She was patron of potters, smiths and weavers as much as of the city's arms.
entities.bio: Born fully armed from the head of Zeus; patron of Athens, of craftsmen and of heroes.
entities.longBio: Zeus, warned that Metis would bear a son greater than his father, swallows her while she is pregnant; the child grows inside him until Hephaestus splits his skull and Athena leaps out fully armed with a war cry. Having no mother in the ordinary sense and remaining a virgin, she stands outside the marriage-and-descent logic that governs most of the pantheon. Her war is not Ares' war: she represents generalship, discipline and the tactical mind, and the two are explicitly contrasted in the Iliad, where she twice helps wound him. She is the standing patron of heroes who think - Odysseus above all, but also Perseus, Heracles and Diomedes. She wins Athens by producing the olive tree against Poseidon's spring. Her severity is real: she turns Arachne into a spider for winning a weaving contest, and blinds Tiresias for seeing her bathe, though she compensates him with prophecy.
entities.variantTraditions: Pallas is variously explained as the name of a childhood companion she accidentally killed and afterwards honoured, or as a word meaning maiden or brandisher. The Romans identified her with Minerva.

entities.name: Apollo
entities.role: God of prophecy, music, healing and plague
entities.abode: Delos, where he was born; Delphi, where he prophesies; Olympus
festivals: Pythian Games at Delphi, every four years
entities.worship: Delphi was the most consulted oracle in the Mediterranean and the seat of the amphictyonic league; Delos was his birth-island and a great pilgrimage centre. Paeans were sung to him against plague and in thanksgiving.
entities.bio: Son of Zeus and Leto; master of the Delphic oracle, of the lyre, and of both plague and its cure.
entities.longBio: Apollo is born on Delos with his twin Artemis, and within days claims the lyre, the bow and the giving of oracles as his own. He takes Delphi by killing the serpent Python that guarded it, and must be purified for the killing - a detail that made Delphi the natural authority on purification from bloodguilt. His oracle spoke through the Pythia in answers so ambiguous he was called Loxias, the oblique, and it was consulted on colonisation, war and law for a thousand years. He holds opposites: the same arrows that bring the plague opening the Iliad also carry healing, and his son Asclepius takes medicine further than Zeus will permit. He is the patron of music and the leader of the Muses, and he flays Marsyas alive for losing a musical contest to him. His loves are conspicuously unsuccessful - Daphne becomes a laurel to escape him, Cassandra takes his gift of prophecy and refuses him, and he kills Hyacinthus by accident with a discus.
entities.variantTraditions: Apollo's identification with Helios the Sun is a later development, common from the fifth century BCE, and absent from Homer and Hesiod. Some accounts have him inherit Delphi peacefully from Phoebe rather than seize it from Python.

entities.name: Artemis
entities.role: Goddess of the hunt, wild places and childbirth
domains: the transition of girls to womanhood
festivals: Brauronia at Brauron, where girls served as 'bears' before marriage
entities.worship: Her sanctuaries stood at the edges of settled land. The temple at Ephesus was one of the seven wonders. Girls approaching marriageable age served her at Brauron, and women dedicated clothing to her after safe childbirth - or, if they died in labour, their clothes were offered to her as well.
entities.bio: Twin of Apollo; virgin huntress, protector of wild things and of women in labour.
entities.longBio: Artemis is born first of the twins and, in a detail the tradition keeps, immediately helps her mother deliver Apollo, which is why a virgin goddess presides over childbirth. She asks Zeus for eternal maidenhood, a bow, a band of nymphs and the mountains to range in. Her protection of the wild is fierce and unsentimental: Actaeon, who sees her bathing, is turned into a stag and torn apart by his own hounds; Agamemnon, who kills a deer in her grove and boasts, must offer his daughter Iphigenia before the fleet can sail for Troy, though in many versions Artemis substitutes a deer at the last moment and carries the girl away. She kills Niobe's daughters as Apollo kills the sons. She also kills Orion, by accident or by design depending on the version, and Callisto for breaking her vow of chastity. Alongside this severity she was the ordinary Greek girl's goddess, presiding over the passage out of childhood.
entities.variantTraditions: The Artemis of Ephesus, with her many-breasted or many-egged image, is an Anatolian mother goddess assimilated to the Greek name and quite unlike the huntress. The Romans identified her with Diana.

entities.name: Ares
entities.role: God of war's violence
entities.abode: Thrace, in the Greek imagination; Olympus
entities.worship: Cult of Ares was thin in most of Greece and vigorous in Sparta and Thrace; dogs and sometimes captives were his offerings in the harshest traditions reported by later writers.
entities.bio: God of the killing itself, disliked by gods and men, and the least successful Olympian in a fight.
entities.longBio: Ares is the son of Zeus and Hera, and Zeus tells him plainly in the Iliad that he is the most hateful of all the gods, because strife and war and battles are always dear to him. He represents the violence of combat rather than the conduct of war, which is Athena's, and the tradition consistently humiliates him: Athena knocks him down with a boulder, Diomedes wounds him with her help and he bellows like ten thousand men and runs to complain to Zeus, and the Aloadae giants once stuffed him into a bronze jar for thirteen months. His long affair with Aphrodite is exposed when Hephaestus traps them in an unbreakable net and invites the gods to laugh. Yet he is not a joke everywhere: in Sparta and in Thrace his cult was serious, he fathered the Amazons, and the Areopagus in Athens was named for his trial there for killing a son of Poseidon who had assaulted his daughter - the first murder trial.
entities.variantTraditions: Roman Mars is a far more dignified figure than Ares, an agricultural protector and father of Romulus, and the identification flatters the Greek god considerably.

entities.name: Aphrodite
entities.role: Goddess of love, beauty and desire
entities.abode: Cyprus, where she came ashore; Olympus
festivals: Adonia, a women's festival mourning Adonis
entities.worship: Her greatest sanctuaries were at Paphos on Cyprus and Cythera. She was invoked by brides, by sailors for calm seas, and at Corinth in a cult that later writers associated with sacred prostitution, a claim modern scholars treat with caution.
entities.bio: Born from the sea-foam about Ouranos' severed flesh; the power of desire that no one resists.
entities.longBio: Hesiod derives Aphrodite from the foam gathered about the genitals of Ouranos when Cronus threw them into the sea, which makes her older than Zeus and independent of his line; Homer instead calls her the daughter of Zeus and Dione. She comes ashore at Cyprus, and grass springs where she walks. Her power is compulsion: her embroidered girdle contains desire so complete that Hera borrows it to distract Zeus. She is married to Hephaestus, the lame smith, and conducts a long affair with Ares. The Judgement of Paris turns on her, when she outbids Hera's offer of power and Athena's of victory by promising Paris the most beautiful woman alive, and the resulting abduction of Helen causes the Trojan War. Her own griefs are real: she loves the mortal Adonis and cannot save him from the boar, and she is wounded by Diomedes at Troy while rescuing her son Aeneas.
entities.variantTraditions: The Greeks themselves distinguished Aphrodite Urania, heavenly and spiritual love, from Aphrodite Pandemos, common or physical love, a division Plato makes much of in the Symposium. Her cult shows clear influence from the Near Eastern Ishtar and Astarte. The Romans identified her with Venus.

entities.name: Hephaestus
entities.role: God of the forge, fire and craftsmanship
entities.abode: A forge beneath Lemnos, or under Etna; Olympus
festivals: Hephaisteia at Athens, with torch races
entities.worship: Strongest at Athens, where the temple above the agora still stands, and on volcanic Lemnos. Smiths and metalworkers were his people, and he was honoured alongside Athena as the pair who gave mortals the arts.
entities.bio: The smith of the gods, thrown from Olympus and lame, who makes everything of consequence.
entities.longBio: Hera bears Hephaestus alone, in some accounts in retaliation for Athena's motherless birth, and casts him from Olympus in disgust at his lameness; he falls for a day, is taken in by Thetis and Eurynome, and learns his craft in a sea cave. In another version Zeus throws him down for taking Hera's side. He takes revenge by sending Hera a golden throne that traps her, and refuses to free her until Dionysus gets him drunk and brings him back to Olympus on a donkey, a scene Greek vase-painters loved. His work is behind most of the tradition's important objects: Zeus' sceptre and aegis, Achilles' shield, Helios' chariot, Pandora herself, the chains that hold Prometheus, and the automata of gold that assist him in the forge. He is the only Olympian who works, and the only one with a visible disability, and the pairing is not accidental - the tradition ties his craft to his exclusion.
entities.variantTraditions: The two accounts of his fall are inconsistent and were both current. The Romans identified him with Vulcan, whose cult was more concerned with destructive fire than with craft.

entities.name: Hermes
entities.role: Messenger of the gods; guide of souls, thieves and travellers
festivals: Hermaia, with athletic contests for young men
entities.worship: Herms stood before houses, at crossroads and at boundaries throughout Attica. He was the patron of merchants, heralds, travellers and, frankly acknowledged, thieves, and received the last offering at many symposia.
entities.bio: Born at dawn and a thief by midday; the god who crosses every boundary, including death's.
entities.longBio: The Homeric Hymn to Hermes gives the most engaging birth story in Greek myth: born in a cave on Cyllene in the morning, he is out of his cradle by midday, invents the lyre from a tortoise shell he finds at the door, then steals Apollo's cattle, driving them backwards so the tracks mislead, and is back in his swaddling clothes feigning innocence by evening. Brought before Zeus, he lies so charmingly that Zeus laughs, and he settles with Apollo by trading the lyre for the cattle. That story fixes his character: he is the god of crossing lines - between properties, between countries, between languages, between the living and the dead. He guides souls down to Hades, which no other Olympian does, escorts Persephone back up, and is the one sent when Zeus needs something delicate handled. His stone markers, herms, stood at Athenian doorways and crossroads, and their mutilation on the eve of the Sicilian expedition was a political scandal that helped ruin Alcibiades.
entities.variantTraditions: Hermes Trismegistus, the syncretic Greco-Egyptian figure of the Hermetic writings, merges him with Thoth and belongs to a much later esoteric tradition. The Romans identified him with Mercury.

entities.name: Dionysus
entities.role: God of wine, ecstasy and the theatre
entities.abode: Everywhere his rites are held; Olympus, where he takes Hestia's seat in some accounts
festivals: City Dionysia at Athens, where tragedy and comedy were performed
entities.worship: His rites ranged from the civic grandeur of the Athenian dramatic festivals to the mountain revels of the maenads. Wine, the mask and the thyrsus were his instruments, and his festivals licensed a temporary suspension of ordinary social order.
entities.bio: Born twice, from Semele and then from Zeus' thigh; the god who dissolves the boundaries of the self.
entities.longBio: Semele, pregnant by Zeus, is tricked by a disguised Hera into asking him to appear in his true form; the lightning kills her, and Zeus sews the unborn child into his thigh until it can be born. Raised in hiding, Dionysus wanders as far as India spreading the vine, driving those who refuse him mad. His arrival is never comfortable. Pentheus of Thebes forbids his rites and is torn apart by his own mother in her ecstasy; the daughters of Minyas refuse and are driven insane; pirates who seize him find the mast sprouting vines and leap overboard as dolphins. He is the last god admitted to Olympus and the only one born of a mortal mother, and he goes down to Hades to bring Semele up and make her a goddess. His cult is the origin of the theatre: Athenian tragedy and comedy were performed at his festival, in his precinct, with his priest in the front seat, which is why the two great dramatic forms belong to the god of losing yourself.
entities.variantTraditions: The Bacchae of Euripides is the fullest and most unsettling treatment of his arrival. Orphic tradition tells a different birth, as Zagreus, son of Zeus and Persephone, torn apart by the Titans and reborn - a story central to Orphic teaching about the human condition.

entities.name: Hestia
entities.role: Goddess of the hearth and of the household's centre
entities.abode: The hearth of every house and of every city
entities.worship: Every meal began and ended with an offering to her. The civic hearth in the prytaneion burned perpetually, and a colony's legitimacy depended on fire carried from its mother city's hearth.
entities.bio: Eldest child of Cronus, who gave up her Olympian throne and kept the hearth instead.
entities.longBio: Hestia is the first of Cronus' children swallowed and the last disgorged, which the Greeks turned into a formula: she is first and last, and receives the first and last portion at every sacrifice. Courted by Poseidon and Apollo, she refused both and asked Zeus to let her remain a virgin and keep the hearth, and he granted it along with the central place in every home. She has almost no mythology, and that is the point. She does not travel, quarrel, take lovers or intervene; she stays. Her fire was the practical and symbolic centre of the household, and the public hearth in the prytaneion was the centre of the city, from which colonists carried embers to light the hearth of a new settlement. In several lists she yields her place among the twelve to Dionysus, which is usually read as the settled order making room for the disruptive one.
entities.variantTraditions: Whether Hestia or Dionysus counted among the twelve varied by place and period; the Romans identified her with Vesta, whose Vestal Virgins tended a state fire whose extinction was a national emergency.

entities.name: Hades
entities.role: Lord of the dead; ruler of the world below
entities.abode: The house of Hades, below the earth
entities.worship: Very few temples; his rites were chthonic, with black victims, offerings poured into trenches and faces turned away. He was invoked in curses and in oaths sworn by the dead.
entities.bio: Zeus' brother, who drew the underworld by lot; a stern rather than evil king.
entities.longBio: Hades receives the world below when the brothers divide the cosmos, and thereafter almost never leaves it. He is not a devil and not a tormentor: he administers, he keeps what is his, and the tradition's consistent complaint about him is not cruelty but implacability. The Greeks were wary of naming him and preferred Plouton, the wealthy one, both because the dead outnumber the living and because what grows and what is mined come from below. His one great action is the abduction of Persephone, carried out with Zeus' consent, which produces the arrangement of the seasons. He is otherwise moved only rarely: he permits Orpheus to lead Eurydice out on a condition, is compelled by Heracles to release Cerberus for a time, and is tricked by Sisyphus. His helm of invisibility, made by the Cyclopes, is lent to Perseus and to gods in battle. There were almost no temples to him, and offerings made to him were poured into pits rather than burned upward.
entities.variantTraditions: Because the Greeks avoided his name, Plouton became so standard that the Romans took it as Pluto; the association of underworld wealth also blurred him with Plutus, god of riches, who is a different figure.

entities.name: Persephone
entities.role: Queen of the underworld; the returning grain
entities.abode: The underworld for part of the year; the upper world with Demeter for the rest
entities.worship: Worshipped with Demeter as the Two Goddesses, most importantly at Eleusis. Her return was the emotional centre of the Mysteries, and initiates were promised a better condition among the dead.
entities.bio: Demeter's daughter, carried off by Hades and returned on terms that divide the year.
entities.longBio: Gathering flowers in a meadow, Persephone reaches for a narcissus and the earth opens; Hades takes her below in his chariot. Demeter's search and strike force Zeus to negotiate her return, but she has eaten pomegranate seeds in the underworld, and whoever eats there belongs there, so she must return for part of each year. The Greeks read the arrangement as the seed that must go under the ground before it can come up. Her double character is unusually sharp: as Kore, the Maiden, she is the girl in the meadow; as Persephone she is the dread queen whom Odysseus fears, who grants and withholds the passage of shades, and who rules beside Hades with real authority. She adjudicates the dispute between Aphrodite and Demeter over Adonis, is moved by Orpheus' music into granting his request, and turns the nymph Minthe into the mint plant for approaching her husband.
entities.variantTraditions: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter is the fullest account and gives four months below; Ovid and others give six. In Orphic tradition she is the mother of Zagreus by Zeus, which places her at the centre of Orphic anthropology. The Romans called her Proserpina.

entities.name: Hecate
entities.role: Goddess of crossroads, witchcraft and the boundary of worlds
entities.worship: Deipna, suppers of food, were left for her at crossroads at the new moon. Small shrines called hekataia stood before doorways as protection, and she was invoked in binding spells and curse tablets.
entities.bio: Titan-descended goddess honoured by Zeus above all others, who moves freely between the three realms.
entities.longBio: Hesiod gives Hecate an extraordinary passage of praise, saying Zeus honoured her above all and left her a share in earth, sea and starry sky - unusual attention for a figure of her rank, and possibly reflecting a local Boeotian cult. She is the daughter of Perses and Asteria, and so a Titan by descent who nonetheless keeps her privileges under the new order. She alone hears Persephone's cry and, torch in hand, helps Demeter search, afterwards becoming Persephone's attendant, which makes her the one figure at home in both the upper and lower worlds. From the classical period she accumulates the associations she is now best known for: the crossroads, where her suppers were left on the new moon and where the poor took them; the practice of magic, so that Medea and Circe are her devotees; and the company of ghosts and howling dogs. She is shown in triple form, facing three ways at once.
entities.variantTraditions: Her early dignified aspect and her later sinister one sit uneasily together, and modern treatments often assume only the latter. She was widely conflated with Artemis and Selene as a lunar triad from the Hellenistic period.

entities.name: Thanatos
entities.role: Death itself
entities.abode: Tartaros, in the house he shares with Sleep
entities.bio: Personified death, twin of Sleep, whose heart of iron and bronze knows no pity.
entities.longBio: Thanatos is born of Nyx without a father, twin to Hypnos, and Hesiod draws the contrast between them sharply: Sleep is gentle and kind to men, while Thanatos has a heart of iron and a spirit of bronze, and once he takes a man he does not let go, so that he is hateful even to the deathless gods. He is not the ruler of the dead, which is Hades' office, but the act of dying, and in the Iliad he and Hypnos together carry the body of Sarpedon from the battlefield to Lycia, which is his most sympathetic appearance. Twice he is defeated. Sisyphus binds him in chains so that no one on earth can die until Ares frees him; and Heracles wrestles him at the tomb of Alcestis to win her back for Admetus, a scene Euripides dramatises. Those defeats are the tradition's way of registering how exceptional it is for anyone to escape him.
entities.variantTraditions: Roman writers call him Mors. Later art shifts him from a bearded man to a beautiful winged youth with a lowered torch, which is the version that influenced European funerary sculpture.

entities.name: Hypnos
entities.role: Sleep
epithets: Lord of All Gods and All Men
domains: dreams by way of his sons
entities.abode: A cave in the land of the Cimmerians where the sun never reaches; or Lemnos
entities.bio: Twin of Death, the gentle brother, who can put even Zeus to sleep.
entities.longBio: Hypnos is the kind twin, and the Greeks noted that he is the only power who overcomes everyone nightly without violence. He lives in a cave through which the river Lethe runs and where no cock crows and no dog barks, and he is the father of the Oneiroi, the dreams, of whom Morpheus, who takes human shape in dreams, is the best known. Twice Hera enlists him against Zeus. The first time he puts Zeus to sleep so she can persecute Heracles, and when Zeus wakes he hunts Hypnos through heaven and would have thrown him into the sea had Hypnos not fled to his mother Nyx, whom Zeus would not offend. The second time, in the Iliad, Hypnos bargains hard, refusing until Hera promises him Pasithea, one of the Graces, as a wife; then he lulls Zeus so the Greeks can push the Trojans back from the ships.
entities.variantTraditions: Roman writers call him Somnus, and Ovid's description of his cave in the Metamorphoses is the fullest ancient account. The number and names of his sons vary.

entities.name: Charon
entities.role: Ferryman of the dead
domains: the crossing of the Styx or Acheron
the boundary the dead must pay to cross
entities.bio: The ferryman who carries the dead across, for a fee, and only if they have been buried.
entities.longBio: Charon poles his boat across the Acheron or the Styx carrying the shades of the dead, and he takes only those whose bodies have received burial rites and who can pay. The fee is the reason for the Greek and later Roman practice of placing a small coin, an obol, in the mouth of the dead. Those left unburied wander the near bank for a hundred years before he will take them, which is why proper burial is such an insistent concern in Greek tragedy - Antigone's whole crisis turns on it. He refuses the living. Heracles forces a passage from him and Charon is punished for it by a year in chains; Aeneas is admitted only when the Sibyl shows him the golden bough. He is a minor figure in Homer, who does not mention him, and grows in importance in later literature and in vase painting on funerary vessels, becoming one of the most familiar images of death in the Mediterranean world.
entities.variantTraditions: Charon is absent from Homer entirely and first appears in later archaic poetry; his prominence is greatest in the Roman period, and Virgil's Aeneid VI gives the description that shaped Dante and everything after.

entities.name: The Erinyes
entities.role: The Furies; avengers of kindred blood
domains: vengeance for murder within a family
entities.abode: Beneath the earth; the cave below the Areopagus at Athens
entities.worship: A sanctuary of the Semnai stood in a cleft below the Areopagus at Athens, where offerings were made without wine.
entities.bio: Born from the blood of Ouranos; they pursue those who shed the blood of kin.
entities.longBio: The Erinyes rise from the drops of Ouranos' blood that fell on Gaia, which makes them older than the Olympians and not subject to them. Their jurisdiction is narrow and absolute: bloodshed within a family, offences against parents, and perjury. They cannot be reasoned with and they do not weigh circumstances, which is precisely the problem Aeschylus builds the Oresteia around. Orestes kills his mother Clytemnestra because she killed his father, at Apollo's express command, and the Erinyes hound him mad regardless, because to them the only relevant fact is matricide. The trilogy ends with the first homicide trial, a hung jury, Athena's casting vote for acquittal, and - crucially - the Erinyes being persuaded rather than defeated: they accept a place of honour beneath Athens and are renamed the Eumenides, the Kindly Ones. That resolution is one of the tradition's clearest statements about the passage from vendetta to law.
entities.variantTraditions: Their number is not fixed in early sources; the three names Alecto, Megaera and Tisiphone are later. The euphemistic names Eumenides and Semnai were used out of fear of naming them directly.

entities.name: The Moirai
entities.role: The Fates; the three who measure a life
domains: the allotted span of a life
entities.abode: Beyond the reach of the gods
entities.bio: The three who spin, measure and cut the thread of every life, and whom even Zeus does not overrule.
entities.longBio: Clotho spins the thread of a life, Lachesis measures out its length, and Atropos cuts it. Their authority is the one genuine limit on Zeus, and the Iliad shows him confronting it: he wishes to save his son Sarpedon, and Hera tells him that if he does, the other gods will each save their own favourites and the order of things will fail. Zeus weeps tears of blood and lets Sarpedon die. Hesiod gives them two genealogies without reconciling them - daughters of Nyx alone in one passage, daughters of Zeus and Themis in another - and the inconsistency reflects a real tension over whether fate stands outside the divine order or is administered within it. Apollo once cheats them for Admetus by getting them drunk and extracting a promise that he could live if another died in his place, which is the premise of Euripides' Alcestis, and even that concession requires a substitution rather than an exemption.
entities.variantTraditions: The Romans identified them with the Parcae. The Norse Norns occupy a strikingly similar position, which comparative mythology has long noted.

entities.name: Nike
entities.role: Victory
domains: victory in war and in contest
entities.abode: At the side of Zeus and Athena
entities.bio: Winged victory, daughter of Pallas and Styx, who stands beside Zeus and Athena.
entities.longBio: Nike is the daughter of the Titan Pallas and of Styx, and when Styx brought her children to Zeus at the start of the Titanomachy she was the first to declare for him. Zeus rewarded that early loyalty by keeping Nike and her siblings Kratos, Bia and Zelos permanently at his side. She is less a character than an attribute: she is regularly shown small, held in the hand of Zeus or Athena, or flying to crown a victor. The gold-and-ivory Athena in the Parthenon held a Nike in her right hand, and the temple of Athena Nike stands on the Acropolis bastion. Her most famous surviving image, the Winged Victory of Samothrace, was set up to commemorate a naval battle. The Romans took her as Victoria, whose altar in the Senate house became the centre of one of the last public disputes between paganism and Christianity.
entities.variantTraditions: Athena Nike at Athens was shown wingless, and later writers explained this as an attempt to keep victory from flying away from the city.

entities.name: Iris
entities.role: Messenger of the gods; the rainbow
entities.bio: The rainbow personified; the gods' messenger, particularly Hera's.
entities.longBio: Iris is the daughter of Thaumas and the Oceanid Electra, and sister of the Harpies. She carries messages where Hermes is not sent, and in the Iliad she is the busier of the two, running errands for Zeus and above all for Hera. The rainbow is her path, joining sky to earth, which fits her function exactly. One duty is peculiar to her: when a god must swear the great oath, Iris fetches water from the Styx in a golden pitcher, and a god who swears falsely by it lies breathless for a year and is cut off from the councils of the gods for nine more. Unlike Hermes she does not conduct souls and does not deal in trickery; she is simply fast and reliable. She is sometimes given as the wife of Zephyrus, the west wind, and mother of Pothos, longing.
entities.variantTraditions: In later poetry Iris is increasingly a servant of Hera specifically rather than of the gods generally, and Virgil has her sent to release the dying from their bodies, a function with no Greek precedent.

entities.name: Eris
entities.role: Strife
domains: the quarrel that starts a war
entities.bio: Discord, whose golden apple set the Judgement of Paris in motion.
entities.longBio: Hesiod, unusually, splits Eris in two: one Strife is the cruel sort who fosters war and quarrel, born of Nyx, and the other is the wholesome kind that makes a farmer work harder when he sees his neighbour prospering. It is the first who acts in myth. Not invited to the wedding of Peleus and Thetis - the one union of a goddess and a mortal the gods sanctioned - she throws a golden apple among the guests inscribed to the fairest. Hera, Athena and Aphrodite each claim it, Zeus refuses to judge, and the decision is put to the Trojan prince Paris, whose choice of Aphrodite and her bribe of Helen brings on the Trojan War. That single act makes her the efficient cause of the largest story in Greek literature, and it is a precise piece of characterisation: she does not fight, she simply introduces a comparison.
entities.variantTraditions: The inscription on the apple and the detail of the uninvited guest are not in Homer; they come from the epic cycle and later summaries. The Romans called her Discordia.

entities.name: Nemesis
entities.role: Retribution against excess
domains: the correction of undeserved good fortune
entities.abode: Rhamnous in Attica, where her great temple stood
entities.worship: Her temple at Rhamnous in Attica held a celebrated statue attributed to Agoracritus, and she was invoked against those whose prosperity seemed unearned.
entities.bio: The power that corrects excess, especially the arrogance of those who have too much good fortune.
entities.longBio: Nemesis is born of Nyx and personifies the distribution of what is due. Her concern is not crime in the legal sense but disproportion: the man whose fortune outruns his deserving, or whose success makes him forget his condition, attracts her attention. She carries a measuring rod and a bridle, and her name comes from a verb meaning to give what is owed. The Greeks paired her closely with hybris, and the reason her cult at Rhamnous mattered is a story about the Persians: they were said to have brought a block of marble to Attica to make a victory monument, and after Marathon the Athenians carved it into her statue instead. In one mythological strand she is pursued by Zeus, changes shape to escape him, is caught as a goose, and lays the egg from which Helen hatches, which makes the cause of the Trojan War her daughter.
entities.variantTraditions: The competing tradition makes Leda rather than Nemesis the mother of Helen; some accounts have Nemesis lay the egg and Leda find it.

entities.name: Tyche
entities.role: Fortune, good and bad
entities.abode: Wherever chance operates; the citadel of each city
entities.bio: The fortune of individuals and cities, who steers with a rudder and is blind to desert.
entities.longBio: Tyche stands for what happens rather than what is deserved, and her rise is a good index of a change in Greek thinking. She is barely present in Homer and Hesiod, and becomes one of the most worshipped figures of the Hellenistic world, when the sudden rise and fall of kingdoms made luck seem the governing principle. She holds a rudder, because she steers events, and a cornucopia, because she can pour out abundance; later she stands on a wheel or a ball, to show how unsteady she is. Each city had its own Tyche, wearing a crown shaped like the city walls, and the Tyche of Antioch became one of the most copied statues in antiquity. Greek writers distinguished her sharply from the Moirai: the Fates allot an unalterable span, while Tyche gives and takes without pattern.
entities.variantTraditions: The Romans took her as Fortuna, whose wheel passed into medieval literature as the wheel of fortune and from there into European art and poetry.

entities.name: Eros (son of Aphrodite)
entities.role: The archer of desire
domains: the arrow that cannot be resisted
entities.bio: The later, younger Eros: a winged archer whose arrows cause specific loves.
entities.longBio: This Eros is the son of Aphrodite - by Ares, Hermes or Zeus depending on the source - and is a quite different figure from the primordial Eros of the Theogony. He is a boy or youth with a bow, and his arrows cause particular people to fall in love, which makes him a narrative device rather than a cosmic principle. Ovid gives him the two arrows that shape one of the best-known stories: a golden one that kindles love, shot into Apollo, and a lead one that repels it, shot into Daphne, so that the god pursues and the nymph flees until she becomes a laurel. His own story is the tale of Cupid and Psyche in Apuleius, in which he falls in love with a mortal girl, visits her only in darkness, and abandons her when she lights a lamp to see him, after which she must complete a series of impossible tasks set by a jealous Aphrodite before they are reunited and she is made immortal.
entities.variantTraditions: The two Eros figures were recognised as distinct in antiquity and argued over in Plato's Symposium. The Roman Cupid or Amor derives from this younger version, and is the ancestor of the modern cherub.

entities.name: Pan
entities.role: God of flocks, wild places and sudden fear
entities.worship: Worshipped in caves and grottoes rather than temples, most anciently in Arcadia and after Marathon in a cave on the north slope of the Athenian Acropolis. Shepherds offered him milk and honey.
entities.bio: Goat-legged god of shepherds, inventor of the panpipes, and source of the word panic.
entities.longBio: Pan is an Arcadian god, usually called the son of Hermes, with the horns, ears and legs of a goat. He haunts wild upland country, sleeps at noon and resents being woken, and pursues nymphs with mixed success: Syrinx flees him and is turned into reeds, from which he cuts the panpipes that carry her name, and Echo rejects him and is torn apart or fades to a voice. The sudden groundless terror that can seize a flock, or an army at night, was attributed to him, and is the origin of the word panic; he was credited with causing exactly that among the Persians at Marathon, after which Athens gave him a cave shrine below the Acropolis. Plutarch preserves a strange and much-discussed story that a sailor passing Paxi heard a voice command him to announce that the Great Pan was dead, and that when he did so a great lamentation was heard from the shore.
entities.variantTraditions: Pan's name was later connected, probably wrongly, with the Greek word for all, which encouraged Orphic and Stoic writers to make him a universal nature god. The Romans identified him with Faunus.

entities.name: Asclepius
entities.role: God of medicine and healing
domains: the cure that comes in sleep
entities.abode: Epidaurus; and among the stars as Ophiuchus
festivals: Asclepieia at Epidaurus, with games every four years
entities.worship: Healing sanctuaries at Epidaurus, Kos, Pergamon and Athens practised incubation, in which patients slept in the abaton and were treated in dreams. Non-venomous snakes were kept in the precincts, and cockerels were a common thank-offering.
entities.bio: Son of Apollo, so skilled a healer that he raised the dead, and was killed by Zeus for it.
entities.longBio: Apollo's mortal lover Coronis is unfaithful while pregnant; Apollo kills her but snatches the child from the pyre and gives him to the centaur Chiron, who teaches him medicine. Asclepius surpasses his teacher and eventually learns to raise the dead, in one account using blood from the Gorgon's veins given him by Athena. Zeus kills him with a thunderbolt, because the boundary between the living and the dead cannot be crossed without unravelling the order of things; Apollo, unable to strike back at Zeus, kills the Cyclopes who made the bolt and is punished with a year's servitude to a mortal. Asclepius is afterwards raised to divine status. His cult was the most practical in Greece: the sick slept in his sanctuaries and reported dreams in which he appeared and prescribed or operated, and hundreds of inscribed thanksgivings survive from Epidaurus.
entities.variantTraditions: His daughters Hygieia, health, and Panacea, all-cure, are personifications who acquired cults of their own. The single-serpent staff of Asclepius is frequently and incorrectly replaced in modern medical usage by the two-serpent caduceus of Hermes.

entities.name: Eileithyia
entities.role: Goddess of childbirth
entities.worship: The cave at Amnisos and a sanctuary at Olympia were her chief sites; women dedicated clothing and figurines after safe deliveries.
entities.bio: The goddess who attends births, and whose absence prevents them.
entities.longBio: Eileithyia is the daughter of Zeus and Hera and the power that permits a birth to complete. Her importance is shown most clearly by what happens when she is withheld: Hera keeps her from Leto for nine days and nights so that Apollo cannot be born, until the other goddesses bribe her with a necklace nine cubits long, and Hera similarly detains her to delay the birth of Heracles while hastening that of Eurystheus, so that the prophecy about the child born that day falls to the wrong boy. In that story a servant tricks the goddess into unclasping her hands, and the birth proceeds. Her cult is very old: a cave at Amnisos in Crete shows continuous use from the Neolithic, and her name appears on Linear B tablets, which makes her one of the few Greek deities attested before the alphabet.
entities.variantTraditions: Sometimes there are two Eileithyiai rather than one, and from the classical period her functions are increasingly absorbed by Artemis and by Hera Eileithyia.

entities.name: Hebe
entities.role: Goddess of youth; cupbearer to the gods
entities.bio: Daughter of Zeus and Hera, who poured the nectar and became the wife of Heracles.
entities.longBio: Hebe is youth in the sense of the physical prime, and she served nectar and ambrosia to the gods until Ganymede replaced her. Her real significance is as the reward at the end of the greatest of the labours: when Heracles dies on the pyre and his divine part is taken up to Olympus, he is reconciled with Hera and given Hebe in marriage, which resolves the enmity that had driven his whole career. She has the power to restore youth and does so at Heracles' request for his nephew Iolaus, granting him one day of his former strength to fight. Her cult was modest, attached chiefly to Heracles' sanctuaries, though at Phlius she had a grove where suppliants were given asylum and the freed prisoners hung their chains on the trees.
entities.variantTraditions: The Romans identified her with Juventas, who presided over the assumption of the adult toga.

entities.name: The Muses
entities.role: The nine who inspire poetry, music and knowledge
epithets: Calliope, Clio, Erato, Euterpe, Melpomene, Polyhymnia, Terpsichore, Thalia, Urania
entities.worship: Sanctuaries on Helicon, where the Mouseia games were held, and in Pieria. Poets and schools honoured them, and libraries and philosophical schools were often formally dedicated to them.
entities.bio: Nine daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne, who give poets what they could not otherwise know.
entities.longBio: The Muses are born of Zeus and Memory on nine successive nights, and Hesiod opens the Theogony with an account of meeting them on Helicon, where they gave him a staff of laurel and breathed a divine voice into him, telling him bluntly that they know how to speak many false things as though they were true, but also how to utter true things when they choose. That warning is one of the earliest Greek statements about the unreliability of inspired speech. Their function is practical in an oral culture: the poet asks them for material he cannot have witnessed, which is why the Iliad and the Odyssey both open by asking a goddess to sing or to tell. The division into named specialities - Calliope for epic, Clio for history, Urania for astronomy and so on - is a late systematisation. Mortals who challenge them lose badly: Thamyris is blinded and stripped of his skill, and the daughters of Pierus are turned into magpies.
entities.variantTraditions: Earlier traditions give three Muses rather than nine, and Pausanias records both counts with their different names. The Alexandrian Mouseion, the institution behind the Library, is named for them and gives us the word museum.

entities.name: The Charites
entities.role: The Graces; givers of charm and delight
domains: the pleasure of gratitude given and returned
entities.bio: Three goddesses of charm and grace who attend Aphrodite and adorn the world.
entities.longBio: The Charites are usually three - Aglaia the splendid, Euphrosyne the cheerful and Thalia the flourishing - and are given as daughters of Zeus and the Oceanid Eurynome. They attend Aphrodite, weave and perfume her robes, and appear wherever the tradition wants to signal grace rather than power. Their name is the same word as charis, which covers charm, favour and the gratitude owed for a favour, and that range matters: the Greeks understood grace as something that circulates rather than something merely possessed, which is why the Graces are conventionally shown dancing in a ring with hands joined. Aglaia is given as the wife of Hephaestus in the Theogony, an arrangement that sits oddly with his marriage to Aphrodite elsewhere. Hypnos is promised the Grace Pasithea as the price of drugging Zeus.
entities.variantTraditions: Their number and names vary; some cities honoured two, and the Spartans and Athenians gave different names. Seneca's discussion of why they dance in a ring became a standard text on the reciprocity of favours.

entities.name: Nereus
entities.role: The Old Man of the Sea
epithets: The Old Man of the Sea
entities.bio: Eldest son of Pontos, prophetic and incapable of lying; father of the fifty Nereids.
entities.longBio: Hesiod introduces Nereus by saying he is trusty and gentle, does not forget what is right, and knows just and kindly counsels - an unusual endorsement in the Theogony, and one that marks the older sea powers as different in character from the Olympians who displaced them. With the Oceanid Doris he fathers the fifty Nereids, among them Thetis and Amphitrite. Like several sea gods he is prophetic and will change shape violently to avoid answering, so that the way to consult him is to hold on through the transformations: Heracles does exactly this to learn the way to the garden of the Hesperides. He appears in art at the wedding of his daughter Thetis and in scenes of Heracles' struggle. He does not oppose the Olympians and is not displaced by them; he simply continues.
entities.variantTraditions: Proteus, Phorcys and Glaucus are similar old sea figures with overlapping traits, and ancient writers sometimes confused them.

entities.name: Proteus
entities.role: The shape-shifting seer of the sea
epithets: The Old Man of the Sea
entities.abode: The island of Pharos, off Egypt
entities.bio: A prophetic sea god who changes shape to avoid answering, and must be held fast.
entities.longBio: Proteus herds the seals of Poseidon and knows all things, past and present, but will not tell willingly. In the Odyssey, Menelaus is becalmed in Egypt and is advised by Proteus' own daughter to ambush him at noon while he sleeps among his seals, and to hold on however he changes; Proteus becomes a lion, a serpent, a leopard, a boar, running water and a tree before giving up and answering, telling Menelaus how to get home and what became of his companions at Troy. Virgil gives a closely parallel scene in which Aristaeus wrestles him for the reason his bees have died. The pattern of pinning a shifting sea power to force the truth is one of the most durable in Greek myth, and gives English the word protean.
entities.variantTraditions: Some accounts make Proteus a king of Egypt rather than a sea god, and Herodotus reports an Egyptian tradition in which Helen spent the war at his court while a phantom went to Troy - a version Euripides dramatised.

entities.name: Amphitrite
entities.role: Queen of the sea
domains: the calm and swell of water
entities.bio: A Nereid who fled Poseidon's suit and was persuaded back by a dolphin.
entities.longBio: Amphitrite is one of the fifty daughters of Nereus and Doris. Pursued by Poseidon, she fled to Atlas at the edge of the world; Poseidon sent messengers after her, and a dolphin found her and argued his case so persuasively that she consented, for which the dolphin was set among the stars. She becomes queen of the sea and mother of Triton. Her role in myth is mostly that of a consort, and the tradition gives her few actions of her own, though in some accounts she is responsible for turning Scylla into a monster out of jealousy, using poisoned herbs in the pool where Scylla bathed. In art she rides beside Poseidon in a chariot drawn by hippocamps, attended by Nereids and tritons, and by the Roman period she is often barely distinguished from a personification of the sea itself.
entities.variantTraditions: The jealousy story is also told of Circe rather than Amphitrite. The Romans identified her with Salacia.

entities.name: Thetis
entities.role: Sea-nymph; mother of Achilles
entities.abode: The depths, with her father Nereus; Phthia during her marriage
entities.bio: The Nereid whom Zeus dared not marry, given to a mortal, whose son was Achilles.
entities.longBio: Thetis is the most consequential of the Nereids because of a prophecy: Themis, or Prometheus, knew that any son she bore would be greater than his father. Zeus and Poseidon both desired her, and on learning this they married her off to the mortal Peleus, whose wedding all the gods attended and where Eris threw the golden apple. Peleus had to win her by holding on while she changed into fire, water, a lion and a serpent, the same pattern as with Proteus. She tried to make her son Achilles immortal, in the best-known version by dipping him in the Styx while holding his heel. When his death is fated she cannot prevent it, and the Iliad turns on what she can do instead: she goes to Zeus and secures a promise that the Greeks will suffer until her son's honour is restored, and later brings him new armour made by Hephaestus. She had earlier sheltered Hephaestus when he was cast from Olympus and Dionysus when he fled Lycurgus.
entities.variantTraditions: The dipping in the Styx and the vulnerable heel are not in Homer, who never mentions Achilles being invulnerable; they appear in later sources, most fully in Statius.

entities.name: Calypso
entities.role: The nymph of Ogygia
domains: the island out of the world
entities.bio: The nymph who kept Odysseus seven years and offered him immortality, which he refused.
entities.longBio: Calypso, daughter of Atlas, lives alone on Ogygia in a cave surrounded by alder, poplar and cypress, with four springs and a great vine. Odysseus, shipwrecked and the last of his crew, washes ashore and remains seven years. She offers to make him immortal and ageless if he will stay, and the Odyssey is careful to record that he spends his days on the shore weeping for home while spending his nights with her against his will. Athena raises the matter in the gods' council and Hermes is sent to order his release; Calypso complains bitterly and accurately that the gods resent goddesses taking mortal lovers while doing as they please themselves, then gives Odysseus tools, timber and provisions to build a raft. Her name means the one who conceals, and her episode is the clearest statement in the poem of what Odysseus is choosing when he chooses to go home: mortality, and his own wife and life.
entities.variantTraditions: Later writers gave her a son or sons by Odysseus, but Homer does not. Her island's location was debated in antiquity and never settled.

entities.name: Circe
entities.role: The enchantress of Aeaea
epithets: The Dread Goddess Who Speaks with Human Voice
entities.bio: Daughter of Helios; a goddess of drugs and transformation who turned Odysseus' men into swine.
entities.longBio: Circe is a daughter of Helios and the Oceanid Perse, and sister of Aeetes and Pasiphae, a family with a marked association with sorcery. On Aeaea she lives in a stone house surrounded by wolves and lions who fawn rather than attack, because they are men she has transformed. She drugs Odysseus' scouting party and turns them into swine, keeping their human minds; Odysseus, protected by the herb moly given him by Hermes, resists the drug and forces her to swear an oath not to harm him. She then becomes a helper rather than an obstacle, restoring his men, entertaining them for a year, and giving the sailing directions that make the rest of the voyage possible - including the instruction to go down to the dead first, and the warnings about the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis and the cattle of Helios. She also appears in the Argonautica, where she purifies Jason and Medea, her niece, for the murder of Apsyrtus.
entities.variantTraditions: Later tradition, especially Ovid, expands her transformations considerably, including turning Scylla into a monster and Picus into a woodpecker.

entities.name: The Cyclopes
entities.role: The three smiths who forged the thunderbolt
domains: thunder and lightning as manufactured things
entities.abode: Beneath the earth, at the forge; later under Etna
entities.bio: One-eyed sons of Gaia and Ouranos, who gave Zeus the thunderbolt and were freed to do it.
entities.longBio: Hesiod's Cyclopes are three: Brontes the thunderer, Steropes the lightning-maker and Arges the bright, each with a single round eye, and each a craftsman of enormous skill. Ouranos imprisoned them, and Cronus left them imprisoned after taking the throne; Zeus freed them, and in return they made him the thunderbolt, Poseidon the trident and Hades the helm of invisibility - which is to say that the three weapons that decide the Titanomachy come from a group the previous two rulers had chosen to lock away. Later they work as Hephaestus' assistants. Apollo kills them in revenge for the thunderbolt that killed Asclepius, and is punished for it. They are entirely distinct from the pastoral Cyclopes of the Odyssey, of whom Polyphemus is one: those are lawless one-eyed herdsmen with no craft at all, and the tradition never reconciled the two groups.
entities.variantTraditions: The Hesiodic smiths and the Homeric shepherds are effectively different beings sharing a name; later writers sometimes merged them by making the shepherds descendants of the smiths.

entities.name: The Hecatoncheires
entities.role: The Hundred-Handed Ones
entities.bio: Three brothers with a hundred arms and fifty heads each, whose released force ended the Titanomachy.
entities.longBio: Briareus, Cottus and Gyges are the last children of Gaia and Ouranos, each with fifty heads and a hundred arms, and their father shut them away in the earth from the first out of loathing and fear. Cronus, having overthrown Ouranos, kept them confined. In the tenth year of the Titanomachy, when neither side could gain the advantage, Gaia told Zeus that victory lay with them; he went down, revived them with nectar and ambrosia, and brought them up. They threw three hundred rocks at once and buried the Titans beneath the missiles, and afterwards were set as the guards of Tartaros where the Titans are held - jailers who had been prisoners. Homer records a separate detail: when Hera, Poseidon and Athena once plotted to bind Zeus, Thetis fetched Briareus to sit beside him, and the sight of him was enough that the gods gave up the attempt.
entities.variantTraditions: Homer says the gods call him Briareus while men call him Aegaeon, one of several places where the epics distinguish divine from human names.

entities.name: Typhon
entities.role: The last challenger to Zeus
domains: the last revolt against the Olympian order
entities.bio: Gaia's last child, a hundred-headed storm monster who nearly overthrew Zeus.
entities.longBio: Gaia bears Typhon to Tartaros as her final answer to the defeat of the Titans, and Hesiod describes a creature with a hundred serpent heads from its shoulders, eyes flashing fire, and voices that variously bellow like a bull, roar like a lion, yelp like puppies or hiss. Had Zeus not acted quickly, Hesiod says, Typhon would have ruled gods and men. In Apollodorus' fuller and stranger version the fight goes badly first: Typhon catches Zeus, cuts out the sinews of his hands and feet, and hides him in a cave in Cilicia guarded by a she-dragon, until Hermes and Aegipan steal the sinews back and restore him. Zeus then pursues him with thunderbolts and finally throws Mount Etna on top of him, which is why the mountain burns. With Echidna he fathers most of the great monsters: Orthrus, Cerberus, the Hydra, the Chimera and, in some accounts, the Sphinx and the Nemean lion.
entities.variantTraditions: Egyptian syncretism identified Typhon with Set, and one strand of the story has the gods flee to Egypt and hide in animal form, which was used to explain Egyptian animal-headed deities - a Greek rationalisation rather than an Egyptian belief.

entities.name: Echidna
entities.role: Mother of monsters
domains: the borderland between beast and woman
entities.abode: A cave in the Arima, deep under the earth
entities.bio: Half beautiful woman, half speckled serpent; consort of Typhon and mother of the great monsters.
entities.longBio: Hesiod places Echidna in a hollow cave, a creature in nothing like mortal men or the deathless gods: half a nymph with glancing eyes and fair cheeks, half a monstrous serpent, terrible and enormous, eating raw flesh beneath the secret parts of the holy earth. She neither dies nor grows old. With Typhon she bears Orthrus the two-headed hound, Cerberus, the Lernaean Hydra and the Chimera, and in various later accounts the Sphinx, the Nemean lion, the Caucasian eagle that ate Prometheus' liver, and the dragon of the Hesperides. She therefore stands behind a large share of the labours of Heracles and the trials of other heroes, without ever acting herself. Apollodorus says she was killed in her sleep by Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed watchman, for the habit of seizing passers-by.
entities.variantTraditions: Her parentage is inconsistent across sources: Hesiod's text is ambiguous, and she is variously the daughter of Phorcys and Ceto, of Tartaros and Gaia, or of Chrysaor and Callirhoe.

entities.name: Medusa
entities.role: The Gorgon whose gaze turns to stone
entities.abode: An island in the far west, beyond the ocean
entities.bio: The only mortal Gorgon, beheaded by Perseus; her head kept its power afterwards.
entities.longBio: The three Gorgons are daughters of Phorcys and Ceto; Stheno and Euryale are immortal, and Medusa alone can be killed, which is why she is the one the story is about. Perseus, sent for her head, is equipped by Athena and Hermes with a mirrored shield, winged sandals, the helm of invisibility and a sickle, and beheads her while she sleeps, looking only at her reflection. From her severed neck spring the winged horse Pegasus and the giant Chrysaor, her children by Poseidon. Perseus uses the head as a weapon - it works on the dead as well as the living - and finally gives it to Athena, who fixes it on the aegis. The gorgoneion, the face alone, was one of the commonest protective images in Greece, on shields, roof tiles and ovens, on the principle that a face terrible enough to petrify will turn away whatever is coming.
entities.variantTraditions: Ovid supplies the version most familiar now, in which Medusa was a beautiful woman raped by Poseidon in Athena's temple and punished by Athena with the snakes - a Roman moralisation absent from the Greek sources, where the Gorgons are simply born monstrous.

entities.name: Cerberus
entities.role: The hound of Hades
domains: guarding the gate of the dead
entities.bio: The three-headed dog who lets the dead in and none out.
entities.longBio: Cerberus is a child of Typhon and Echidna, usually with three heads, a serpent for a tail and snakes along his back. His job is precise and asymmetrical: he fawns on those entering and devours anyone attempting to leave, which makes him the enforcement of the underworld's one rule. Only a handful get past him. Orpheus lulls him with music; the Sibyl drugs him with a honeyed cake for Aeneas, which is the origin of the phrase about a sop to Cerberus; Heracles, in the twelfth and last labour, is permitted by Hades to take him provided he uses no weapons, and wrestles him into submission, carrying him up to show Eurystheus, who hides in a jar at the sight, before returning him. Where his slaver fell on the earth, the poisonous plant aconite was said to have grown.
entities.variantTraditions: The number of heads varies: Hesiod gives fifty, Pindar a hundred, and most art and later literature three.

entities.name: The Lernaean Hydra
entities.role: The many-headed serpent of the marsh
entities.abode: The marshes of Lerna, near Argos
entities.bio: The serpent that grew two heads for every one cut off, killed by Heracles with fire.
entities.longBio: The Hydra, offspring of Typhon and Echidna and raised by Hera specifically as a trial for Heracles, lives in the swamp at Lerna beside a spring that was believed to be an entrance to the underworld. Its problem is structural rather than one of raw strength: cutting a head produces two more, so effort makes it worse. Heracles solves it by cooperation, having his nephew Iolaus cauterise each neck with a burning brand as soon as the head is severed, and by burying the one immortal head under a rock. Hera sends a giant crab to hamper him, which he crushes and she sets among the stars. He then dips his arrows in the Hydra's blood, which makes them incurably poisonous - a decision that echoes through the rest of his life, since those arrows accidentally wound Chiron and Pholus, and eventually cause his own death by way of the centaur Nessus. Eurystheus refused to count the labour because Iolaus helped.
entities.variantTraditions: Head counts range from five to a hundred across sources; Apollodorus gives nine, which became conventional.

entities.name: The Chimera
entities.role: The fire-breathing composite of Lycia
symbols: a goat rising from the back
entities.bio: Lion in front, goat in the middle, serpent behind, breathing fire; killed by Bellerophon.
entities.longBio: Homer describes the Chimera as of divine stock, not of men, in front a lion, behind a serpent and in the middle a goat, breathing out the terrible force of blazing fire. It is a child of Typhon and Echidna, and it ravages Lycia until Iobates, wanting Bellerophon dead, sends him against it as a certain death sentence. Bellerophon, mounted on the winged horse Pegasus, attacks from above where the fire cannot reach him, and in the version Apollodorus reports kills it by fixing a lump of lead to his spear and thrusting it into the creature's mouth, where its own fire melts the metal and it suffocates. The Chimera's name became the ordinary Greek and later English word for an impossible hybrid or a delusion, and a natural gas seep in Lycia that burns continuously is still called Yanartas and was associated with it in antiquity.
entities.variantTraditions: Hesiod gives it three heads rather than the composite body Homer describes, and art shows both arrangements.

entities.name: The Sphinx
entities.role: The riddler of Thebes
domains: the price of a wrong answer
entities.bio: Woman-headed lion who strangled those who could not answer her riddle, until Oedipus did.
entities.longBio: The Greek Sphinx, unlike the Egyptian, is female, winged, and lethal. Sent against Thebes by Hera or Ares, she sat on a rock outside the city and put a riddle to every traveller, strangling those who failed - her name comes from a verb meaning to squeeze. The riddle, which is not given in the earliest sources but is standard by the Hellenistic period, asks what goes on four legs in the morning, two at noon and three in the evening; the answer is a human being, crawling, walking, and walking with a stick. Oedipus answers correctly, and the Sphinx throws herself from her rock. His reward is the throne of Thebes and marriage to the widowed queen Jocasta, who is his mother, so that solving the riddle is precisely the act that completes the prophecy he had fled to avoid. A second riddle, about two sisters who give birth to each other, appears in some accounts.
entities.variantTraditions: The Greek Sphinx is unrelated in function to the Egyptian one, which is male, wingless and guardian rather than predatory; the shared name reflects Greek visitors applying a familiar word.

entities.name: The Minotaur
entities.role: The bull of Minos in the labyrinth
symbols: a bull's head on a man's body
entities.bio: Bull-headed son of Pasiphae, kept in the labyrinth and fed on Athenian youths.
entities.longBio: Minos prays to Poseidon for a bull to sacrifice as a sign of his right to rule Crete; a magnificent white bull comes from the sea and Minos keeps it instead of killing it. Poseidon's punishment is to make Minos' wife Pasiphae desire the animal, and Daedalus builds her a hollow wooden cow so that the union can take place. The child is the Minotaur, whose proper name is Asterion, and Daedalus is then set to build the labyrinth to contain him. Athens, defeated in war, is required to send seven youths and seven maidens at intervals to be given to the creature. Theseus volunteers among them, and with the thread given him by Ariadne finds his way in, kills the Minotaur and finds his way out again. The story sits on top of real Cretan bull imagery - the bull-leaping frescoes and the horns of consecration at Knossos - which the Greeks reinterpreted through their own narrative logic.
entities.variantTraditions: Some sources make the Minotaur simply a cruel man named Taurus, a rationalising version reported by Plutarch alongside the mythological one.

entities.name: Scylla
entities.role: The six-headed terror of the strait
domains: the loss that cannot be avoided
entities.abode: A cliff in the strait, opposite Charybdis
entities.bio: A cliff-dwelling monster who takes six sailors from every ship that passes.
entities.longBio: Scylla lives in a cave high in a cliff on one side of a narrow strait, with twelve dangling feet and six long necks each ending in a head with three rows of teeth, and a girdle of yelping dogs' heads about her waist - her name is connected with a word for puppy. Opposite her is the whirlpool Charybdis. Circe tells Odysseus plainly that there is no way through without loss and that he must hug Scylla's cliff and accept losing six men rather than risk the whirlpool taking the whole ship, and advises him not to arm against her because she is not a mortal evil but a deathless one. He does as told, and watching her snatch six of his crew is the most pitiable thing he says he saw in all his wanderings. Later writers gave her a backstory as a beautiful nymph transformed by a jealous rival, Circe or Amphitrite, who poisoned the pool where she bathed.
entities.variantTraditions: The transformation story is Hellenistic and Roman; Homer simply presents her as a monster. The pairing with Charybdis gives the proverb about being caught between two dangers.

entities.name: Polyphemus
entities.role: The Cyclops blinded by Odysseus
entities.abode: A cave on the island of the Cyclopes
entities.bio: One-eyed giant herdsman whose blinding brought Poseidon's anger on Odysseus.
entities.longBio: Polyphemus is a son of Poseidon and belongs to the lawless pastoral Cyclopes, who sow nothing, hold no assemblies and have no laws. Odysseus and twelve men enter his cave and are trapped when he blocks the entrance with a boulder no mortals could move; he eats two of them at a time. Odysseus gives him strong wine, tells him his name is Nobody, and when the giant is asleep drives a sharpened, fire-hardened olive stake into his single eye. The other Cyclopes, hearing him roar that Nobody is killing him, conclude he needs no help. The men escape tied beneath the bellies of his rams. The episode turns on a final mistake: Odysseus, safely offshore, cannot resist shouting his real name, which lets Polyphemus pray to his father by name for vengeance, and it is that prayer which keeps Odysseus from home for ten years.
entities.variantTraditions: A gentler Polyphemus appears in Hellenistic poetry, notably Theocritus, as a lovesick giant courting the sea-nymph Galatea; Ovid combines the two by having him crush her lover with a rock.

entities.name: The Sirens
entities.role: The singers whose song is fatal
symbols: a bird's body with a woman's head
entities.abode: An island meadow among the rocks
entities.bio: Bird-bodied singers whose song draws sailors onto the rocks; passed by Odysseus bound to the mast.
entities.longBio: The Sirens sit in a flowery meadow surrounded by the heaped bones of men who have rotted where they landed. What they offer in Homer is not beauty or love but knowledge: they call to Odysseus by name and promise that whoever listens goes on wiser, for they know everything that happened at Troy and everything that happens on earth. Circe's instruction is to stop the crew's ears with wax and, if he wants to hear it himself, to have himself lashed to the mast with orders to tighten the ropes if he begs to be released - which he does. The Argonauts pass differently: Orpheus simply plays louder and more beautifully, and only one man goes overboard. A tradition held that the Sirens would die if anyone passed them, and that they threw themselves into the sea after one of these failures.
entities.variantTraditions: Homer does not describe their appearance or say how many there are; the bird-body is from later art, and the shift to fish-tailed mermaids is medieval, which is why several modern European languages use the word for mermaid.

entities.name: Tiresias
entities.role: The blind prophet of Thebes
entities.abode: Thebes; and afterwards the underworld, where he keeps his mind
entities.bio: Blinded and given prophecy; the only shade in Hades who retains his wits.
entities.longBio: Two stories explain Tiresias. In one he strikes a pair of coupling snakes and is turned into a woman for seven years, then restores himself the same way; called on later to settle a dispute between Zeus and Hera about which sex enjoys love more, he answers on the evidence and Hera blinds him for it, while Zeus compensates with long life and prophecy. In the other he sees Athena bathing and she blinds him, then, unable to undo it, cleans his ears so he can understand the speech of birds. He advises Thebes over seven generations, and his role in tragedy is consistently that of the man who tells the truth to someone who does not want it: he knows what Oedipus has done and resists saying so until forced, and he warns Creon and Pentheus, both of whom ignore him and are destroyed. Odysseus travels to the land of the dead specifically to consult him, because Persephone allowed him alone to keep his understanding after death.
entities.variantTraditions: The number of years spent as a woman and the details of the transformation vary; Ovid gives the fullest version of the snake story.

entities.name: Cassandra
entities.role: The prophet no one believes
entities.bio: Daughter of Priam, given prophecy by Apollo and cursed never to be believed.
entities.longBio: Apollo gives Cassandra the gift of prophecy in the hope of winning her; when she refuses him he cannot take the gift back, so he adds to it that no one will ever believe her. She therefore knows exactly what is coming and is powerless in the most complete way available. She warns that Paris will destroy the city, that the wooden horse holds men, that Troy will fall; she is thought mad and in some accounts locked up. When the city falls she is dragged from the altar of Athena by Ajax the Lesser, a sacrilege that costs the Greeks dearly on the voyage home. Taken as Agamemnon's prize to Mycenae, she stands outside the palace in Aeschylus' Agamemnon and describes in detail the murder about to happen inside, including her own, to a chorus that hears and does not act. She goes in anyway, knowing.
entities.variantTraditions: Some accounts give the gift instead to her and her twin Helenus as children, when temple serpents licked their ears.

entities.name: Calchas
entities.role: Seer of the Greek army
entities.bio: The Greek army's prophet, whose readings drive several of the war's hardest decisions.
entities.longBio: Calchas is the best of augurs, knowing what is, what will be and what was before. He interprets the omen at Aulis of the snake devouring nine sparrows as meaning the war will last nine years and be won in the tenth, and it is he who declares that Artemis is angry and that Agamemnon must sacrifice his daughter Iphigenia before the fleet can sail - a reading that sets the whole chain of the house of Atreus in motion. At Troy he identifies the plague in the opening book of the Iliad as Apollo's anger over the priest's daughter, and only speaks after Achilles guarantees his safety, knowing Agamemnon will resent it. He also determines that Troy cannot fall without Achilles, without the bow of Philoctetes, and without Neoptolemus. A prophecy said he would die when he met a better seer; meeting Mopsus after the war and losing a contest of divination, he died of grief.
entities.variantTraditions: His readings are always correct and always costly, which is part of the tradition's general view that knowing the future does not help much.

entities.name: Heracles
entities.role: The greatest of heroes; performer of the twelve labours
entities.abode: Thebes, Tiryns and everywhere; afterwards Olympus
entities.worship: Unusually, Heracles received both hero-cult, with offerings poured into the ground, and god-cult with burnt sacrifice, and some sanctuaries did both on the same day. He was patron of gymnasia and of soldiers.
entities.bio: Son of Zeus and Alcmene, driven by Hera through twelve labours and finally made a god.
entities.longBio: Zeus fathers Heracles on Alcmene by taking her husband's form, and Hera's hostility begins before birth: she delays his delivery so that Eurystheus is born first and inherits the kingship the prophecy promised, and sends serpents to his cradle, which the infant strangles. Later she drives him mad, and he kills his own wife Megara and their children; the labours are imposed as expiation, twelve tasks set by Eurystheus. He kills the Nemean lion and wears its skin, burns the Hydra's necks, captures the Ceryneian hind and the Erymanthian boar, cleans the Augean stables in a day by diverting rivers, drives off the Stymphalian birds, takes the Cretan bull, the mares of Diomedes, the belt of Hippolyta and the cattle of Geryon, fetches the apples of the Hesperides, and brings Cerberus up alive. His death is domestic rather than heroic: the centaur Nessus, dying of a poisoned arrow, tricks Deianeira into keeping his blood as a love charm, and the robe she sends burns him so that he builds his own pyre. His mortal part burns away and the divine part is taken to Olympus, where he is reconciled with Hera and married to Hebe.
entities.variantTraditions: The order and membership of the labours vary between sources; Eurystheus refused to count the Hydra because Iolaus helped and the stables because Heracles took payment. The Romans knew him as Hercules and gave him an important early cult at Rome.

entities.name: Perseus
entities.role: Slayer of Medusa; founder of Mycenae
entities.bio: Son of Zeus and Danae, who beheaded Medusa and rescued Andromeda.
entities.longBio: Acrisius of Argos, told by an oracle that his daughter's son would kill him, shuts Danae in a bronze chamber; Zeus reaches her as a shower of gold, and mother and infant are set adrift in a chest. Washed up on Seriphos, they are taken in, and when the king Polydectes wants Danae he gets rid of Perseus by demanding the head of Medusa as a gift. Athena and Hermes equip him; he forces the Graeae, three sisters sharing one eye and one tooth, to reveal the way, and beheads Medusa using her reflection. Flying home he sees Andromeda chained to a rock as a sacrifice to a sea monster, kills the monster and marries her.
