He turns Polydectes to stone with the head, gives the head to Athena, and later kills Acrisius by accident with a discus at games, fulfilling the prophecy exactly as the attempt to prevent it made possible. He founds Mycenae and is ancestor of the line that produces Heracles.
entities.variantTraditions: Ovid supplies the elaborations most familiar now, including Atlas being turned to stone and the coral formed from Medusa's blood.

entities.name: Theseus
entities.role: Killer of the Minotaur; founder-king of Athens
symbols: the sword and sandals under the rock
entities.worship: Cimon brought bones identified as Theseus' to Athens around 475 BCE and built the Theseion; the Theseia festival honoured him as the city's founder.
entities.bio: The Athenian national hero, who killed the Minotaur and unified Attica.
entities.longBio: Theseus is raised in Troezen and, on reaching manhood, lifts the rock under which his father Aegeus left a sword and sandals. He travels to Athens by the dangerous land route rather than by sea, killing a series of bandits on the way by the methods they used on others - Procrustes, who fitted travellers to his bed by stretching or cutting, is the best remembered. In Athens he volunteers for the tribute sent to Crete, and with Ariadne's thread finds his way through the labyrinth, kills the Minotaur and returns. He abandons Ariadne on Naxos, and forgets to change his black sail for a white one, so that Aegeus sees it and throws himself into the sea. As king he is credited with the synoecism, the political unification of the villages of Attica into one state, which made him the Athenian democracy's founding figure. His later career is less admirable: he abducts the young Helen, and helps his friend Pirithous attempt to abduct Persephone, for which both are held fast in the underworld until Heracles frees Theseus.
entities.variantTraditions: Plutarch's Life of Theseus treats him as a historical king and carefully sorts what he considers credible from what he does not. The abandonment of Ariadne is variously explained as forgetfulness, cruelty, or Dionysus' claim on her.

entities.name: Jason
entities.role: Leader of the Argonauts
entities.bio: Leader of the voyage for the Golden Fleece, who won it with Medea's help and then betrayed her.
entities.longBio: Pelias, who usurped Iolcus, is warned to beware a man wearing one sandal; Jason arrives having lost one crossing a river, and Pelias sends him for the Golden Fleece in Colchis expecting him not to return. He assembles the Argonauts - the largest gathering of heroes in the tradition, including Heracles, Orpheus, Castor and Polydeuces - and sails through the clashing rocks. Aeetes sets impossible tasks: yoking fire-breathing bulls, sowing dragon's teeth and fighting the armed men that spring up, and taking the fleece from a sleepless serpent. Every one of them is solved by Medea, who has fallen in love with him and whose knowledge of drugs is decisive. She flees with him, murdering her own brother to delay pursuit. Back in Greece she kills Pelias by persuading his daughters to dismember him. In Corinth, Jason sets her aside to marry the king's daughter, and Medea's revenge destroys everything he has. He dies alone, killed by a beam falling from the rotting Argo.
entities.variantTraditions: Apollonius' Argonautica gives the fullest voyage; Euripides' Medea gives the Corinthian ending and made the killing of the children the standard version, though earlier accounts blamed the Corinthians.

entities.name: Achilles
entities.role: The greatest warrior at Troy
domains: the choice between long life and lasting fame
entities.abode: Phthia; the Greek camp at Troy
entities.bio: Son of Thetis and Peleus, whose withdrawal and return are the subject of the Iliad.
entities.longBio: Achilles is offered a choice: a long, obscure life at home, or a short life and undying fame at Troy. The Iliad begins after he has chosen, with Agamemnon taking the captive Briseis from him as a public humiliation. Achilles withdraws from the fighting and asks his mother to persuade Zeus to let the Greeks lose until they understand what he is worth, and the poem then spends most of its length showing exactly what that costs. His friend Patroclus, borrowing his armour to rally the Greeks, is killed by Hector, and Achilles' grief converts into a rage that carries him past every limit: he kills Hector, drags the body behind his chariot, and refuses burial. The poem ends not with a battle but with Priam coming alone into his tent to beg for his son's body, and Achilles, thinking of his own father, giving it back and weeping with him. His own death, by Paris' arrow guided by Apollo, is foretold throughout and falls outside the poem.
entities.variantTraditions: The invulnerability and the fatal heel are not in Homer and come from later sources. The nature of his bond with Patroclus was already debated in the fifth century BCE and is treated differently by different ancient writers.

entities.name: Odysseus
entities.role: The man of many turns
symbols: the bow only he can string
entities.bio: King of Ithaca, deviser of the wooden horse, and subject of the Odyssey's ten-year return.
entities.longBio: Odysseus is the tradition's intelligence rather than its strength, and the Odyssey is explicit that his defining quality is turning - of mind, of speech, of route. He tries to avoid the war by feigning madness and is exposed; at Troy he is the negotiator, the night-raider and finally the author of the wooden horse that ends the siege. The return takes another ten years: the Cicones, the lotus-eaters, Polyphemus, Aeolus' bag of winds opened by his crew in sight of home, the Laestrygonians, Circe, the journey to the dead, the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, the cattle of Helios whose slaughter destroys the last ship, and seven years with Calypso. He reaches Ithaca alone and disguised as a beggar, is recognised only by his old nurse and his dying dog, and kills the suitors who have eaten his household and courted his wife. Penelope tests him even then, ordering their bed moved, which cannot be done because he built it around a living olive tree - a secret only the two of them know.
entities.variantTraditions: Later Greek tragedy often presents him unsympathetically as a sophist and a liar, and Roman writers, identifying with the Trojans, make him worse still. Dante places him in hell for the deception of the horse.

entities.name: Bellerophon
entities.role: Rider of Pegasus; slayer of the Chimera
entities.bio: Tamed Pegasus and killed the Chimera, then tried to ride to heaven and fell.
entities.longBio: Bellerophon is refused by Stheneboea, the wife of King Proetus, who then accuses him of assaulting her. Proetus, unwilling to kill a guest, sends him to his father-in-law Iobates with a sealed message asking that the bearer be put to death - the earliest instance in Western literature of the letter that condemns the man carrying it, and one of very few references to writing in Homer. Iobates likewise will not break hospitality directly and instead sets lethal tasks: the Chimera, the Solymi, the Amazons. Bellerophon, having caught and bridled the winged horse Pegasus with a golden bridle given him by Athena in a dream, survives them all, and Iobates finally gives him his daughter and half the kingdom. Success ruins him. He attempts to ride Pegasus up to Olympus as though he belonged there; Zeus sends a gadfly to sting the horse, Bellerophon is thrown, and Homer leaves him wandering the Aleian plain alone, eating his heart out and avoiding the paths of men.
entities.variantTraditions: Pegasus goes on to Olympus without him and carries Zeus' thunderbolts. Some accounts have Bellerophon lamed or blinded by the fall rather than merely disgraced.

entities.name: Orpheus
entities.role: The singer who went down for his wife
domains: the power of song over nature and the dead
the mystery rites named for him
entities.bio: A singer whose music moved stones and the dead, and who lost Eurydice by looking back.
entities.longBio: Orpheus, son of the Muse Calliope, sings so well that trees uproot themselves to follow, rivers stop and wild animals lie down together. He sails with the Argonauts, where his playing outsings the Sirens and sets the rowing stroke. When his wife Eurydice dies of a snakebite he goes down to the underworld and does what no argument could do: his singing stops the wheel of Ixion, makes Tantalus forget his thirst and brings tears to the Furies, and Hades and Persephone agree to release her on the condition that he not look back until both are in the upper air. Within sight of daylight he turns, and she is drawn back. He refuses all company afterwards and is torn apart by Thracian women, and his severed head, still singing, floats down the Hebrus to Lesbos. The mystery tradition called Orphism took his name and its poems claimed his authorship, teaching a doctrine of the soul's origin and purification quite unlike ordinary Greek religion.
entities.variantTraditions: The condition and the backward glance are given fullest form by Virgil and Ovid; earlier fragments may have allowed him to succeed. Orphic theogonies differ substantially from Hesiod's.

entities.name: Atalanta
entities.role: The huntress who would only marry a man who could outrun her
entities.bio: Exposed at birth and raised by a bear; first to wound the Calydonian boar, and beaten only by trickery.
entities.longBio: Atalanta is exposed as an infant by a father who wanted a son, suckled by a she-bear and raised by hunters. She grows into the fastest runner and one of the finest hunters in Greece, and sails with the Argonauts in some accounts. At the Calydonian boar hunt, called to deal with a monstrous boar sent by Artemis, she draws first blood, and Meleager awards her the hide - a decision that provokes his uncles, whom he kills, which sets off the chain leading to his own death. Reconciled with her father, she is pressed to marry and agrees only on terms: any suitor must beat her in a footrace, and losers are killed. Melanion, or Hippomenes, is given three golden apples by Aphrodite and drops them one at a time during the race; she stops for each and loses. The two are later turned into lions for lying together in a sanctuary, because it was believed lions could not mate with each other.
entities.variantTraditions: Two Atalantas, an Arcadian huntress and a Boeotian runner, appear to have been merged in the tradition, which is why her parentage and details vary.

entities.name: Meleager
entities.role: Leader of the Calydonian boar hunt
domains: the life bound to a burning brand
entities.bio: His life was tied to a log; when his mother burned it in anger, he died.
entities.longBio: When Meleager was a week old the Fates appeared to his mother Althaea and said he would live only until the log then burning on the hearth was consumed; she snatched it out, quenched it, and hid it in a chest. Grown, he gathers the heroes of Greece to hunt the Calydonian boar that Artemis sent because his father had omitted her from a sacrifice. Atalanta draws first blood, Meleager kills the animal and awards her the hide, and when his mother's brothers object and take it from her he kills them. Althaea, hearing that her son has killed her brothers, takes the log from the chest and puts it on the fire, and Meleager dies as it burns. Homer gives a quite different and older version in which there is no log at all: Meleager withdraws from the fighting after his mother curses him, and is persuaded back too late to receive the rewards he was offered - a story Phoenix tells Achilles as a direct warning.
entities.variantTraditions: The Homeric version and the log version are irreconcilable and both remained current; Ovid gives the fullest account of the log.

entities.name: Pandora
entities.role: The first woman
domains: the gift that is a punishment
entities.bio: Made by the gods as a punishment for the theft of fire; opened the jar that released every ill.
entities.longBio: After Prometheus steals fire, Zeus orders a counter-gift. Hephaestus moulds a woman from earth and water, Athena teaches her weaving and dresses her, Aphrodite gives grace and longing, Hermes gives her a shameless mind and deceitful words, and each god contributes something, which is what her name records: all-gifted, or gifted by all. She is sent to Epimetheus, who accepts her despite Prometheus' warning. She lifts the lid of a great jar and out come the sicknesses, sorrows and hard labours that had not existed before, scattering beyond recall; only Hope remains inside under the rim, and Hesiod does not explain whether that is a mercy or the final cruelty, a question readers have argued over ever since. The story is Hesiod's account of why human life is hard, and it is uncomfortably explicit that the woman herself is the punishment.
entities.variantTraditions: The container is a pithos, a large storage jar, not a box; the mistranslation dates to Erasmus in the sixteenth century and has stuck. The Theogony and Works and Days give slightly different accounts, and only the latter names her.

entities.name: Helen
entities.role: The most beautiful woman in the world
epithets: The Face That Launched the Ships
entities.abode: Sparta, then Troy, then Sparta again
entities.bio: Daughter of Zeus by Leda or Nemesis; her departure with Paris began the Trojan War.
entities.longBio: Helen is born from an egg after Zeus comes to Leda as a swan, or in the other tradition to Nemesis, who laid the egg that Leda found. She is abducted as a child by Theseus and recovered by her brothers. When she reaches marriageable age every prince in Greece courts her, and Odysseus proposes the oath that binds them all to defend whoever wins her - which is why the whole of Greece sails when Paris takes her from Menelaus' house. What the tradition never settles is whether she went willingly. Homer shows her in Troy full of self-reproach, calling herself a shameless creature, and also shows the old men of the city agreeing that no one could blame either side for fighting over such a woman. After the fall she returns to Sparta and to Menelaus, and the Odyssey shows the couple receiving guests with an unsettling calm. Stesichorus was said to have been struck blind for slandering her and to have recovered his sight after writing a recantation claiming she never went to Troy at all.
entities.variantTraditions: The phantom tradition, in which only an image of Helen went to Troy while she waited out the war in Egypt, is developed by Herodotus and dramatised by Euripides in his Helen.

entities.name: Paris
entities.role: The prince whose judgement caused the war
entities.abode: Troy; Mount Ida in his youth
entities.bio: Son of Priam, who judged Aphrodite fairest and took Helen as his reward.
entities.longBio: Hecuba dreams while pregnant that she gives birth to a burning torch, and the child is exposed on Mount Ida; a shepherd raises him. Grown, he is chosen to settle the dispute over Eris' golden apple, and each goddess offers a bribe: Hera power, Athena victory in war, Aphrodite the most beautiful woman alive. He chooses Aphrodite, and the resulting abduction of Helen from Menelaus' house brings the Greek fleet. In the Iliad he is a poor figure among fighters - his brother Hector rebukes him for hiding in his bedroom while the city burns for his sake, and Aphrodite has to snatch him out of a duel with Menelaus he is losing. Yet he is the one who finally kills Achilles, with an arrow guided by Apollo to the heel, which the poem treats as the fitting way for the best of the Achaeans to die: not in a fair fight. He is himself killed by the arrows of Philoctetes.
entities.variantTraditions: His alternative name Alexander is older and appears in Hittite records that may refer to him, which is one of the few possible external attestations of a Trojan War figure.

entities.name: Hector
entities.role: Champion of Troy
entities.bio: Priam's eldest son and Troy's defender, killed by Achilles and dragged behind his chariot.
entities.longBio: Hector is the Iliad's most sympathetic figure and its clearest study of duty. He fights not for glory but because the city depends on him, and he knows how it ends: in the scene on the wall with his wife Andromache and their infant son, he tells her plainly that Troy will fall, that she will be taken as a slave, and that he must fight anyway, then reaches for the baby, who is frightened by the plume on his helmet, and laughs and takes it off. He kills Patroclus, and that seals him. When Achilles comes for him he first waits at the gate against his parents' pleading, then breaks and runs three times around the walls before Athena tricks him into standing. Dying, he begs that his body be returned and is refused. Achilles drags him behind the chariot for days until Priam comes alone to the Greek camp to ransom him, and the poem ends with his funeral - not with the fall of Troy, which is deliberate.
entities.variantTraditions: The last line of the Iliad is his epitaph, calling him tamer of horses, which gives the poem's final word to the losing side.

entities.name: Agamemnon
entities.role: Commander of the Greek expedition
domains: the curse on the house of Atreus
entities.abode: Mycenae; the Greek camp at Troy
entities.bio: King of Mycenae who led the Greeks, sacrificed his daughter to sail, and was murdered on his return.
entities.longBio: Agamemnon inherits both a kingdom and a curse: his father Atreus served his brother Thyestes the flesh of his own children, and the consequences run through the family. Becalmed at Aulis, he sacrifices his daughter Iphigenia so the fleet can sail. At Troy his quarrel with Achilles over the captive Briseis opens the Iliad and nearly loses the war, and Homer shows him repeatedly as a man whose authority exceeds his judgement. He returns home in triumph with Cassandra as his prize, and his wife Clytemnestra, who has spent ten years remembering Iphigenia and taking Aegisthus as a lover, welcomes him with purple cloth to walk on and kills him in his bath. That murder is avenged by his son Orestes, whose trial ends the Oresteia and the family's cycle of blood.
entities.variantTraditions: Schliemann's excavation at Mycenae produced a gold funerary mask he named for Agamemnon, though it predates any plausible Trojan War by centuries.

entities.name: Clytemnestra
entities.role: Queen of Mycenae; her husband's murderer
epithets: The Woman with a Man's Mind
domains: the rule of a woman in a husband's absence
entities.bio: Killed Agamemnon on his return in vengeance for their daughter, and was killed by their son.
entities.longBio: Clytemnestra is Helen's sister and Agamemnon's wife, and Aeschylus makes her the most formidable character in his trilogy. Her motive is stated and not concealed: her husband cut their daughter Iphigenia's throat on an altar to buy a wind for his fleet, and she has waited ten years. She governs Mycenae competently in his absence with Aegisthus, sets a chain of beacons across the Aegean to know the moment Troy falls, and greets Agamemnon by spreading crimson cloth for him to walk on - a trap of etiquette, since to tread on it is the arrogance of an eastern king. She kills him in the bath, wrapped in a robe he cannot get his arms out of, and Cassandra with him, and comes out to tell the chorus exactly what she has done and why, refusing to be sorry. Her children Orestes and Electra kill her for it, and her Furies pursue Orestes to Athens.
entities.variantTraditions: Homer's Odyssey gives a shorter version in which Aegisthus is the principal agent and Clytemnestra more passive; the tragedians make her the driver.

entities.name: Penelope
entities.role: Queen of Ithaca; wife of Odysseus
entities.bio: Held off a hundred suitors for years with the trick of the unfinished shroud.
entities.longBio: Penelope holds Ithaca alone for twenty years while suitors occupy the house, eat its stores and press her to declare Odysseus dead and remarry. Her defence is a stratagem worthy of her husband: she says she must first weave a shroud for his father Laertes, and unpicks by night what she weaves by day, sustaining it for three years until a servant betrays her. When the disguised Odysseus finally returns, she does not simply believe him, and the poem is careful about this: she proposes the contest of the bow which only he can string, and then, after the suitors are dead and his identity is being urged on her, she tests him by ordering their marriage bed carried out of the chamber. He objects that it cannot be moved because he built it himself around a living olive tree rooted in the ground, and only then does she accept him. She is the one character in the poem who out-thinks Odysseus.
entities.variantTraditions: A minority tradition, reported disapprovingly by later writers, made her unfaithful and the mother of Pan by all the suitors; it has no basis in Homer.

entities.name: Oedipus
entities.role: The king who solved the riddle and was the answer
domains: the prophecy that fulfils itself through avoidance
entities.abode: Thebes; and Colonus at the end
entities.bio: Killed his father and married his mother without knowing, and blinded himself on learning it.
entities.longBio: Laius of Thebes is told his son will kill him, so the infant's feet are pinned and he is exposed, but he is rescued and raised in Corinth as the king's son. Told by an oracle that he will kill his father and marry his mother, Oedipus leaves Corinth to protect the people he believes are his parents - and on the road kills a stranger in a quarrel at a crossroads, answers the Sphinx's riddle, is given the throne of Thebes and the widowed queen. Years later a plague forces an inquiry into the old king's unsolved murder, and Sophocles' play is the process of Oedipus investigating himself with increasing determination and finding, step by step, that he is what he is looking for. Jocasta hangs herself; he blinds himself with the pins of her brooches and goes into exile. In the later play he arrives at Colonus, an old blind beggar led by his daughter Antigone, and is received into the earth in a way that makes his grave a protection for Athens.
entities.variantTraditions: The oracle's role was already debated in antiquity: nothing compels Oedipus to kill a stranger or marry a widow, and Sophocles is careful that every step is his own decision.

entities.name: Medea
entities.role: Sorceress of Colchis
entities.abode: Colchis, then Iolcus, then Corinth, then Athens
entities.bio: Won the Golden Fleece for Jason, and destroyed everything he had when he set her aside.
entities.longBio: Medea is a granddaughter of Helios and a priestess of Hecate, and every one of Jason's impossible tasks in Colchis is solved by her knowledge: the ointment that makes him fireproof, the trick that turns the sown warriors against each other, the drug that puts the sleepless serpent to sleep. She leaves with him, killing her brother to delay her father's pursuit, and in Iolcus destroys Pelias by demonstrating a rejuvenation on a ram and persuading his daughters to cut him up on the same principle. In Corinth, Jason takes a royal bride, and Euripides' play begins there. Medea sends a poisoned robe and diadem that kill the princess and her father, and then kills her own two sons by Jason - not in madness but as the most complete injury available to a man whose whole future was that marriage - and escapes in a chariot sent by Helios, leaving him with nothing, not even the bodies. She takes refuge in Athens with Aegeus.
entities.variantTraditions: Euripides appears to have introduced the deliberate killing of the children; earlier tradition had the Corinthians kill them, and the play's first audience is said to have been shocked.

entities.name: Ariadne
entities.role: The princess of the thread
entities.bio: Gave Theseus the thread to escape the labyrinth, was abandoned on Naxos, and married Dionysus.
entities.longBio: Ariadne is the daughter of Minos and Pasiphae, and therefore the Minotaur's half-sister. She falls in love with Theseus among the Athenian tribute and goes to Daedalus, who tells her the secret of the labyrinth; she gives Theseus a ball of thread to unwind on the way in and a sword, on condition that he take her with him. He does, and then leaves her sleeping on the island of Naxos. What happens next is where the versions divide most sharply: in the dominant one Dionysus finds her there and marries her, and the crown he gives her is set among the stars as the Corona Borealis, so that the abandonment turns out to be a promotion. Other accounts have her die on the island, or hang herself, or be killed by Artemis. Homer mentions her only briefly and obscurely, and the fuller story is later.
entities.variantTraditions: The reason for Theseus' abandonment is never satisfactorily explained: forgetfulness, a divine command that she was promised to Dionysus, or simple callousness, depending on the source.
